The page closes with: "A compliment is wind, not a finish line. Let it move you, not bind you."

notice-the-present-details.title: The Friendship Detective Solved an Empty Case
notice-the-present-details.teaser: A few short replies become a noir investigation. One direct question reveals moving boxes, early shifts and a phone down the sofa.
paragraphs: The opening treats everyday messaging like a crime thriller. Under slatted golden light, the trench-coated young man stares at his phone while a mug beside him promises, "A CLUE WILL TURN UP." On the next screen, HER replies are only "Sure!," "Mm," "Fine," "OK," and "Got it." Nothing visible proves that the friendship is ending, yet the severe shadows, concentrated pose, desk lamp, and giant phone close-up make those tiny messages feel like coded evidence. The joke comes from that mismatch: the cinematography says major case, while the actual mystery is simply a friend writing shorter replies.

He then commits fully to the detective role. The wall fills with CHAT HISTORY, photos, pinned messages, and notes asking "COLD?," "BUSY?," "AVOIDING ME?," "WHAT HAPPENED?," and even "FRIENDSHIP ENDING?" Red string stretches between the scraps until the evidence literally becomes a butterfly. The visual gag is wonderfully precise: before the facts have formed a pattern, his interpretation already has wings. By panel five he is holding his forehead beside a mug reading "OVERTHINKING IS EXHAUSTING," while the black cat sits quietly at the edge of the desk, looking like the only character who has declined to join the investigation.

The turning point is deliberately small. Instead of finding a secret clue, he types, "Have you been really busy lately?" The lower page then replaces imagined motives with visible circumstances. His friend is surrounded by moving boxes and explains that she has had early shifts, has been moving house, and even lost her phone down the sofa. The man's startled "Down the sofa?!" keeps the scene playful rather than solemn. She then shows him an actual schedule running from a 05:30 early shift through moving, packing, and a 23:00 "EXHAUSTED." In this specific case, the vague fear that she was avoiding him is answered by concrete details from her days.

Once the situation becomes clearer, his behavior changes too. The detective work gives way to box lifting, and a cardboard carton marked "LAST BOX!" replaces the evidence board as the central object. Later, the two sit on the new floor with pizza and mugs and finally talk in full sentences. He says that even a quick heads-up or emoji would help, while admitting that he may still overthink; she answers, "I'll try! Once things settle, let's arrange a proper catch-up." The page does not turn this into a promise that future silence will always mean busyness. It shows two people clarifying one episode and making their expectations a little more explicit.

The final panel brings the whole visual joke back around. The evidence wall is still visible behind him, but the red string is no longer proving a theory; he is wrapping it around a cardboard box. His verdict, "Insufficient evidence. Eight episodes withdrawn," is funny because it reduces an elaborate internal drama to a case that never had enough facts. He then adds, "I'll keep learning about this friendship. Some things take time to understand." That ending connects naturally with the supplied passage from Chapter 14 as a contemporary reflection: deal first with what can actually be checked in the present, then let a longer pattern reveal itself, rather than deciding what silence means before the evidence arrives.
notice-the-present-details.quote: Hold to the Way of the present to deal with what exists in the present; through this, know the ancient beginning. This is called the thread of the Way.
notice-the-present-details.practice: If someone's replies suddenly become shorter, try borrowing one move from the comic: replace one imagined explanation with one specific question, such as "Have you been really busy lately?" Then notice what the next few real interactions, schedules, and responses actually show. One clarification can provide useful context, while a longer pattern still deserves time before you decide what the relationship means.
notice-the-present-details.comicTitle: The Friendship Detective Solved an Empty Case
notice-the-present-details.comicAlt: Two-page Film Noir comic in black-and-gold tones. A trench-coated young man studies a friend's unusually short phone replies, builds a red-string evidence wall whose strings form a butterfly, worries beside a black cat and an "OVERTHINKING IS EXHAUSTING" mug, then asks HER directly whether she has been busy. She appears among moving boxes and explains her early shifts, house move, and phone lost down the sofa, then shows a packed daily schedule. He helps lift the box marked "LAST BOX!," and they later sit on the new floor eating pizza and discussing communication. In the final panel, the evidence wall remains in the background while he wraps the red string around a box and withdraws his imagined eight-episode case.

waiting-for-reply.title: No Reply Yet. I've Already Reached the Finale.
waiting-for-reply.teaser: Ten silent minutes become an imaginary friendship disaster. Her hands are covered in flour; he learns to stop scripting the ending and start making soup.
paragraphs: The opening joke is visible before the man says anything dramatic: the plate of sunflower seeds keeps getting emptier while the phone stays silent. In panels 01 and 02, he begins calmly at the table with "Dinner at mine tonight?" and "I'll make soup," but ten minutes later the black-and-white Op Art spirals seem to accelerate around him. Nothing concrete has happened except the absence of a reply, yet the combination of the nearly empty plate, his worried face, the clock, and the twisting background turns ordinary waiting into a full theatrical production inside his head.

Panels 03 and 04 make that imaginary production deliberately ridiculous. He pictures the bob-haired woman looking annoyed and wonders, "Was that too sudden?" before deciding that his invitation sounds like "a surprise inspection." The next escalation is even bigger: "Have I been blocked?" and "Expelled from the friendship already?" appear beside an obviously imagined phone reading "YOU HAVE BEEN BLOCKED." The exaggerated broken-heart imagery and tunnel-like optical pattern make clear that these are catastrophes he is inventing, not events the woman has actually caused.

The real turning point arrives in panel 05 with three pieces of paper on the table: "NO REPLY," an arrow, and "DOESN'T CARE." Holding his pen, the man asks, "Did I draw that arrow myself?" The joke works because the missing evidence is literally represented by the arrow he supplied. Panel 06 then cuts away from his mental spiral to the woman's actual kitchen. She is smiling in a blue apron, her hands visibly coated in flour, with dumplings lined up in front of her and her phone sitting off to the side. Her line, "Oh, my hands are covered in flour. I'll finish these first," gives this particular delay a simple, practical explanation without pretending that every delayed reply must have one.

The lower page changes the man's behavior instead of giving him another round of speculation. In panel 07 he leaves himself a concrete note, "JUST LET ME KNOW BY 18:00 :)," shoulders a shopping bag, and says, "Buy vegetables first. Stop writing someone else's ending." At the market he chooses a tomato and jokes that "What goes in the soup is easier than what goes on in my head." Meanwhile, the woman finishes the dumplings, washes the flour from her hands, notices the "OLD CLASSMATES" group message, and says, "Finished the dumplings. Only just saw it!" The story's empty waiting time has become useful action on both sides.

The ending brings the two separate routines back together without turning the moment into romance or a grand reconciliation. The woman replies, "I'm in! I'll bring dumplings. You make soup." The man answers "GOT IT!" while adding chopped tomatoes to a steaming pot, and the final panel shows him calmly stirring the soup beneath the line, "The drama in my head is over. Dinner is officially on." The visual rhythm changes too: the earlier warped spirals give way to more regular grids and checkerboards. That makes "When muddied, let it settle in stillness; gradually it becomes clear" a fitting but limited connection to the supplied excerpt: the comic is not translating the ancient line into a universal rule about messaging, but showing one everyday case in which pausing long enough for facts to arrive prevents an unanswered message from becoming a worst-case conclusion.
waiting-for-reply.quote: When muddied, let it settle in stillness; gradually it becomes clear.
waiting-for-reply.practice: The next time a reply is delayed, try writing two separate lines: "What actually happened" and "What I think it means." If you genuinely need an answer, give a clear time by which it would help to hear back, then do one useful task you can finish without checking the phone.
waiting-for-reply.comicTitle: No Reply Yet. I've Already Reached the Finale.
waiting-for-reply.comicAlt: Two-page, twelve-panel Op Art comic about a black-haired man in a gray shirt waiting for a dinner-invitation reply from a bob-haired woman in a blue apron. On the first page he sits with sunflower seeds and a phone as black-and-white spirals intensify around him, imagines that his invitation sounded like a surprise inspection, then imagines being blocked and expelled from the friendship. He finally looks at paper cards reading "NO REPLY → DOESN'T CARE" and realizes he drew the arrow himself. The scene then cuts to the woman actually making dumplings with flour-covered hands while her phone rests nearby. On the second page the man leaves a note asking for a reply by 18:00, goes shopping, and chooses tomatoes while the woman finishes the dumplings and sees the message. She replies that she will bring dumplings and asks him to make soup. He answers "GOT IT!", adds tomatoes to a steaming pot, and ends smiling as he stirs the soup. The closing caption reads, "Don't fill an unanswered message with the worst possible story."

review-a-repeating-week.title: My Weekend Was Bought Out by Catch-Up Sleep
review-a-repeating-week.teaser: A heroic weekend plan collapses into sleep and chores. A friend helps map the whole week, then make room for one small thing he actually wants to do.
paragraphs: The opening joke is built from a sharp visual reversal. On Friday, the man sits at his desk grinning, fist raised beside a notebook headed "Plan," with EXHIBITION, SPORT, COOK SOMETHING GOOD, TIDY ROOM, and MOVIE all waiting neatly to happen. Even the mug cheers "GO FRIDAY!" and the wall insists "LIFE HAS MORE THAN WORK." One panel later, the clock reads 12:00, he is buried under the blue duvet saying, "A little more sleep... just a little...," and the gray-and-white cat is sleeping beside him with complete professional confidence. The poster "SLEEP IS REAL WORK TOO!" makes the contrast even funnier without turning his tiredness into a diagnosis.

The next panels make the cost of the week concrete rather than abstract. The man wakes to a "Weekend Plan" covered in red crossings and asks, "Am I just bad at living?" Then Sunday afternoon puts him in front of the washing machine with a full laundry basket, hanging clothes, detergent, and unfinished household work while he worries that work starts again tomorrow. When the woman in the orange hoodie arrives carrying two drinks, she does not answer that question for him. Instead, after noticing that his weekend posts are "all sleep or worry," she helps move the conversation from self-judgment to observation.

That change of perspective becomes visible through the colorful time blocks. First, the pair map MON through SUN into WORK, COMMUTE, HOUSEWORK & CARE, MEALS & DAILY LIFE, PERSONAL TASKS, and REST & SLEEP. Then the comic turns those categories into a miniature stacked world: FINISHING WORK sits above COMMUTE, SHOPPING & COOKING, FAMILY CARE, MESSAGES, and TIDYING, with tiny figures still doing things inside every level. The visual joke is that his supposed "free time" looks suspiciously like another office building. His line, "Maybe the week was too full," lands because the picture has already shown the accumulation of necessary work and care.

The turning point is deliberately small. The woman suggests, "Drop one optional commitment. Leave breathing room," and the notebook shows WEEKLY ONLINE SESSION crossed out rather than another ambitious goal added. The replacement plan is modest: "WED: EARLY BED" and "WEEKEND: ONE SMALL THING I WANT TO DO." On Wednesday night, the clock reads 22:30 as the man stretches happily in bed and declares, "No overtime tonight. Early sleep. Recharge before the weekend!" The notebook says "SLEEP WELL," while the wall says "TOMORROW CAN BE BETTER." The comic does not pretend that work, commuting, cooking, care, or tidying disappeared; it shows one optional demand being removed so the remaining week has a little more space.

The ending keeps that smaller scale. On Saturday morning, the man does exactly one wanted thing: he takes his camera into the sunshine while the cat lounges nearby beneath the sign "A SMALL JOY IS ENOUGH." By Sunday evening, he and the woman are sitting on the grass with a backpack and bottle beside them, facing the distant city rather than racing through it. He jokes, "Didn't conquer the city. Did get my Saturday back," and she answers that there can be "a little room for what matters, instead of always doing more." Read alongside "All things arise together, and I observe their return.," this works as a contemporary association rather than a literal illustration: the story watches a crowded cycle closely enough to notice where some return, release, and renewed room might become possible.
review-a-repeating-week.quote: All things arise together, and I observe their return.
review-a-repeating-week.practice: Try making a small version of the comic's time-block chart for one ordinary week. Include work, commuting, housework, caring for others, daily tasks, personal tasks, and actual rest. Do not optimize it immediately. First notice what is already taking the space, then see whether one genuinely optional commitment could be paused to leave a little breathing room.
review-a-repeating-week.comicTitle: My Weekend Was Bought Out by Catch-Up Sleep
review-a-repeating-week.comicAlt: Two-page, twelve-panel isometric-style comic about a teal-shirted young man whose ambitious weekend plan collapses into catch-up sleep and chores. The first page shows his Friday checklist, Saturday noon in bed beside a sleeping gray-and-white cat, crossed-out plans, Sunday laundry, an orange-hoodie friend arriving with drinks, and a colorful weekly time-block chart. The second page expands the schedule into miniature stacked scenes labeled finishing work, commute, shopping and cooking, family care, messages, and tidying. They cross out a weekly online session, plan an early Wednesday bedtime, and keep only one wanted weekend activity. He later prepares for bed at 22:30, takes sunny photos on Saturday morning while the cat rests nearby, and ends Sunday evening sitting with his friend in a park overlooking the city.

disagree-gently.title: A Meeting Is Not a Tug-of-War
disagree-gently.teaser: An event-planning meeting turns into a literal tug-of-war. A mediator asks one useful question, and the rope eventually finds a better job: holding both plans.
paragraphs: The opening joke is wonderfully literal. The red-bloused woman wants an event that is fun, interactive, shareable and attractive to younger people, while the blue-shirted man argues that a limited budget makes online promotion safer and easier to control. By panel 03, they are no longer merely comparing ideas: each is pointing at the whiteboard and demanding the main space for a different kind of evidence. Panel 04 turns that territorial argument into an actual rope, with both of them leaning backward and pulling as if the meeting room has become a sports field. The funniest counterpoint arrives in panel 05. Their colleagues are not inspired by the drama at all; one wonders when it will end, while another is simply hungry and wants lunch. The lunch bag, mugs and tired faces gently puncture the grandeur of the contest.

The real turning point is not that one person wins. In panel 06, the gray-dressed mediator steps between them and asks, "What problem are we actually trying to solve?" The next page keeps that question visible by changing the whiteboard into "SHARED GOAL?" and listing three concrete aims: reaching younger people, building brand awareness and staying within budget. That visual shift matters because the board is no longer territory to be claimed by either side. The red-bloused woman then reflects the man's concern back to him, acknowledging that a limited budget spread too thin may do little. His reply confirms that she has understood the fear underneath his position: spending the money and getting nothing. The scene moves from defending a proposal to accurately hearing the concern behind it.

Panel 09 lets the movement go both ways. The blue-shirted man admits that focusing so much on data made him miss the experience, and he recognizes that a memorable event has value within the discussion. The woman does not answer by declaring victory; she simply says, "Then let's combine them." The next panel makes that combination concrete rather than vague. Their board becomes "SMALL PILOT," with one city, a test of the core activity, a controlled budget, feedback collection and a later decision about whether to expand. She says, "Good. Let's do it!" while he proposes starting small and looking at both data and experience. The comic therefore does not erase the disagreement or pretend that every concern has vanished. It turns two valid concerns into a limited experiment whose next step can be observed rather than shouted into existence.

The ending gives the rope joke a satisfying second life. In panel 11, the mediator notes that the pair have moved from opposing sides to an actual plan. The woman calls different perspectives resources, and the man jokes that next time he will listen before claiming the board. Then panel 12 brings back the rope that once represented stubborn pulling. It now stretches calmly across the background as a line holding two sheets: "PLAN A / EXPERIENCE FIRST" and "PLAN B / DATA LED." Neither sheet has been thrown away. The woman and man sit with mugs, smiling, while saying that different opinions do not need a contest in volume and that the energy can go into a better plan. The visual symbol of conflict has not disappeared; its purpose has changed. That small transformation carries the ending more effectively than a sudden speech about perfect harmony would.

The line, "How hesitant they are—how they value their words," can be connected to this story as a contemporary reflection rather than treated as a literal explanation of the comic. The mediator speaks sparingly at the decisive moment: instead of adding another proposal, she asks one question that redirects attention toward the shared problem. After that, the characters do more listening, restating and testing, and less competing for verbal dominance. The comic's closing line, "Different ideas can pull us closer, not farther apart," fits that pattern without claiming that silence itself solves disagreement. A useful connection is that words can carry more weight when they clarify what matters rather than merely occupy more space. That is one possible everyday association with the excerpt, not the only interpretation of the ancient text.
disagree-gently.quote: How hesitant they are—how they value their words.
disagree-gently.practice: When a discussion gets stuck, try one small move before adding another argument: restate the other person's real concern in one sentence, then write down the goal you both accept. If the disagreement remains, consider a limited test that lets both concerns stay visible.
disagree-gently.comicTitle: A Meeting Is Not a Tug-of-War
disagree-gently.comicAlt: Two-page Mid-Century Modern office comic. A red-bloused woman and a blue-shirted man argue over an event plan, literally pull a rope across the meeting room, and bore colleagues who are thinking about lunch. A gray-dressed mediator asks what problem they are solving, leading them to identify shared goals, create a small pilot, and end with the former tug-of-war rope holding two papers labeled "PLAN A / EXPERIENCE FIRST" and "PLAN B / DATA LED".

care-beyond-family-slogans.title: The Busiest Family Member Is Called 'Should'
care-beyond-family-slogans.teaser: Everyone praises mutual understanding while Mom carries the pots. A task list finally puts the family slogan to work—with a splashy first attempt at dishwashing.
paragraphs: The opening joke comes from the gap between the family's words and the work visible around them. In Panel 01, all four family members raise cups over a crowded dinner table framed by red floral patterns, a GOOD FORTUNE diamond, and a FAMILY HARMONY sign while the father declares, "Family means understanding each other!" Panel 02 pushes the contrast further: the father relaxes with his hands behind his head, the son lounges beside him, and everyone warmly agrees that Mom works hardest. Their affection looks genuine, but the nearly cleared table quietly asks who will deal with everything afterward. The comic does not turn anyone into a villain; it lets the comfortable poses, used dishes, and enthusiastic speeches create the contradiction.

Panel 03 delivers the sharpest visual punch line. Mom stands in the kitchen surrounded by steam, holding multiple pieces of cookware while saying, "Plenty of understanding in this family. Apparently no hands." The BETTER TOGETHER sign beside her makes the joke even drier. In the next panel, the daughter looks at her phone, the father scratches his head over a newspaper, and the son looks sheepish while they admit, "She's right...", "I haven't helped much...", and "We left everything to Mom." The turning point is small but important: nobody argues about whether they care. They notice that expressing sympathy has been easier than noticing the actual labor sitting underneath dinner.

The daughter then changes the conversation from a virtue to a list of visible jobs. In Panel 05 she writes HOUSEHOLD TASKS on a board and names groceries, cooking, chopping, washing dishes, cleaning the kitchen, and taking out the trash. The lower page makes that structure even more concrete with SHARE THE WORK: Dad gets dishes, the son gets groceries, the daughter chops, Mom cooks, and everyone tidies. The joke continues through action rather than accusation. Dad's first turn at the sink sends water splashing everywhere, but the daughter answers, "It's okay. First try!" and the son laughs, "Ha! Progress!" Nobody grabs the chore back from him simply because he is inexperienced.

After that, the panels become a sequence of ordinary hands doing ordinary things. The son returns carrying grocery bags and announces, "Fresh groceries are here!" Mom works at a steaming pot and says cooking feels lighter with help, while the daughter keeps chopping at the counter. The cleanup panel spreads responsibility across the whole group at once: the daughter wipes the table, Dad dries dishes, the son holds the trash bag, and Mom carries stacked bowls while saying, "Good! Finish together." These props matter because the comic's change is measurable: bags arrive, vegetables are cut, dishes are dried, rubbish is removed, and the table is reset. Mutual understanding becomes something the viewer can actually see.

The final panel completes the joke without pretending that family life has become perfectly efficient. Mom is finally seated with everyone at a table of hot food and says, "Finally, a hot meal I can sit down for!" Behind them, MUTUAL UNDERSTANDING hangs beside a TODAY'S TASKS board with every role checked off. Dad's line, "The slogan joined the workforce today!", neatly connects the ending to the earlier wall slogans. Read beside Chapter 18, this works best as a contemporary association rather than a literal illustration of the ancient text: the supplied line notices how named family virtues become conspicuous when natural harmony has faltered. The comic explores a modest household version of that tension, suggesting that care becomes more visible when it enters specific shared actions instead of remaining only a word everyone agrees with.
care-beyond-family-slogans.quote: When the six family relationships are not in harmony, there is filial devotion and parental affection.
care-beyond-family-slogans.practice: The next time someone says, "We should all be more understanding," try the daughter's move from the comic: write down the actual tasks that are waiting and let each person claim one small job. Leave room for an imperfect first attempt, like Dad's splashy dishwashing, and notice what changes when a shared value becomes a shared action.
care-beyond-family-slogans.comicTitle: The Busiest Family Member Is Called 'Should'
care-beyond-family-slogans.comicAlt: Two English comic pages in a warm Chinese New Year woodblock-print style show a four-person family moving from cheerful slogans to shared housework. The first page opens with the glasses-wearing father in a green sweater, the son in a red hoodie, the daughter in a red floral sweater, and the headscarf-wearing mother in a floral apron toasting around a full dinner table beneath GOOD FORTUNE and FAMILY HARMONY signs. After everyone talks about understanding Mom, she is shown alone carrying steaming pots and jokes that the family has plenty of understanding but apparently no hands. The daughter creates a household task list. On the second page, the jobs are assigned: Dad washes dishes, the son buys groceries, the daughter chops vegetables, Mom cooks, and everyone tidies. Dad's first dishwashing attempt sends water splashing from the sink while the others encourage him. Later the son brings grocery bags, Mom cooks at a steaming pot, the daughter chops vegetables, and the family wipes the table, dries dishes, removes trash, and carries bowls together. The final panel shows all four seated around a hot meal beneath MUTUAL UNDERSTANDING and a fully checked TODAY'S TASKS board, with Dad joking that the slogan joined the workforce today.

a-gathering-without-performance.title: Dinner with Friends, Almost a Michelin Audition
a-gathering-without-performance.teaser: Matching plates, swan napkins, perfect flowers—and no dinner. Two friends arrive before the stove is on, then turn the grand production into a warm, slightly messy meal.
paragraphs: The opening joke is built from escalation. The curly-haired hostess begins by admiring an elegant table on a screen and declaring that her own dinner has to look just as polished. The scene surrounds her with HOME DESIGN, TABLE LINENS, and DAILY INSPIRATION books, while the display promises that an elegant dinner starts with details. She then returns carrying matching plates, boxes, and shopping bags, and spends more time folding white napkins into swans among candles, pink flowers, crystal glasses, and gold decoration. The visuals become increasingly luxurious while the practical purpose of the evening quietly disappears from view. By panel 03, she can proudly announce that the swan napkins are finished, which is funny precisely because the audience can already sense that the most edible part of dinner has not yet begun.

The wall clock provides the turning point. In panel 04, the hostess stands among piles of vegetables with a wooden spoon and a cookbook titled WHAT'S FOR DINNER?, suddenly realizing that she has not even turned on the stove. The elegant fantasy collapses further when the doorbell goes DING DONG. She meets her guests clutching a bundle of white napkins and jokes that "the swans have clocked off" while "the chef hasn't clocked in." The same doorway beat carries into the lower page, where her two friends answer with laughter rather than judgment: "No problem. We're here to help!" Nothing in their expressions suggests that they came to inspect the table. Their response changes the evening from a performance by one person into something the three of them can make together.

After that, the comic shifts its attention from decoration to hands doing ordinary things. The dark-haired man offers to wash while someone else trims the greens, and the brunette woman laughs that three pairs of hands make the work more fun. Soon the hostess is at the stove cooking eggs in a black frying pan, steam rises from nearby pots, and her friends lean in to watch and taste. The food is deliberately modest: eggs, hot soup, greens, rice, and simple shared dishes. That simplicity becomes the new source of warmth. The man calls the eggs "the smell of home," and the woman says a little hot soup will finish the meal. The joke has moved too: instead of admiring perfect swans, everyone is now enjoying the fact that dinner finally smells like dinner.

At the table, the Rococo setting never disappears; chandeliers, candles, flowers, porcelain bowls, and gold details remain in the background. What changes is the group's relationship to them. The pink tablecloth now has visible sauce marks, bowls and plates are actively being used, and all three friends are laughing while they eat. The man says the meal feels warmer than a restaurant, the hostess happily admits that the night is "a little messy" and "a little improvised," and the brunette friend is already promising to return. Panel 11 turns the remaining imperfection into the final visual gag: the hostess holds up a cloth covered with reddish stains and says even the tablecloth got seasoned. Her friends respond by laughing, stacking dishes, and calling the scene more like real life rather than treating the mess as a failure.

The last panel makes the change concrete with a prop rather than a speech about perfection. The hostess sits beside the fluffy cat and writes in a spiral notebook labeled TONIGHT'S GOAL. PERFECT DINNER has been crossed out beside an empty checkbox, while FRIENDS OVER FOR DINNER is checked and finished with a heart. Her final line says that dinner with friends is not a portfolio review and that having them there is the best part. Read alongside the supplied Chapter 19 excerpt, this can work as a contemporary association with "seeing the plain" and "embracing the uncarved": less effort spent turning hospitality into a display leaves more attention for the people actually present. The comic does not establish that as the only meaning of the ancient passage; it simply stages one everyday situation in which loosening attachment to form makes room for shared experience.
a-gathering-without-performance.quote: These three sayings, taken merely as formulations, are still insufficient; therefore let them have something to which they belong: see the plain, embrace the uncarved; lessen self-interest and reduce desire.
a-gathering-without-performance.practice: For the next casual meal with people you know well, you might try making the first version of the plan deliberately small: one hot dish, one pot of soup, and enough places to sit. Flowers and folded napkins can stay optional. If the schedule slips, inviting everyone into the kitchen may become part of the evening rather than evidence that it went wrong.
a-gathering-without-performance.comicTitle: Dinner with Friends, Almost a Michelin Audition
a-gathering-without-performance.comicAlt: Two-page Rococo-style comic in pink and gold. A curly-haired hostess obsessively prepares an ornate dinner table with matching dishes, candles, flowers, and swan-folded napkins, then realizes late that she has not started cooking. A dark-haired man and a wavy brunette woman arrive, laugh, and help wash greens, cook eggs and soup, and share a simple meal. Sauce stains land on the tablecloth, everyone keeps laughing, and the hostess later crosses out "PERFECT DINNER" in her notebook and checks "FRIENDS OVER FOR DINNER" beside a heart while a fluffy cat sits nearby.

a-weekend-of-your-own.title: My Feed Tours the World. I Water the Plants.
a-weekend-of-your-own.teaser: Jing plans an entire adventure catalog for one weekend, then gets tired just packing. A neighbor’s question helps her keep the activities she actually wants.
paragraphs: The opening joke is wonderfully concrete: Jing is sitting in a bright, plant-filled room with her phone while her feed seems to be speed-running the planet. One post says "WEEKEND SKYDIVE!", another celebrates a summit, and another announces a gallery day with a "soul recharged." Even her mug quietly insists that "GOOD LIFE IS EVERYDAY," yet she feels as though everyone else's weekend is happening somewhere she forgot to attend. Her answer is immediate and comic: she creates a "WEEKEND PLAN" packed with skydiving, hiking, an art show, a craft workshop, a city bike ride, and camping, as if a sufficiently long checklist could manufacture a more exciting life.

The plan becomes funny in a different way once preparation begins. Jing has not even stepped outside, but the room is already buried under a backpack, helmet, water bottle, camera, shoes, clothes, and other gear while the orange cat sleeps through the entire logistical crisis. With one hand on her head, she admits that packing alone feels like a workout. Then the beige-overalls neighbor appears with a mug and jokes, "Jing, off this early? Conquering the world?" The real turn arrives in the next panel when he asks, "Do you want to go—or just want people to know you went?" Jing's small "...Huh?" lands because the question interrupts the momentum without mocking travel itself.

The lower page shows the change through actions rather than a dramatic rejection of activity. Jing opens "MY ACTIVITIES" and cancels skydiving, hiking, the art show, the city bike ride, and camping, while deliberately keeping the craft workshop. Her relieved "Whew... Lighter already!" makes the point visible: she is editing the schedule, not abandoning the world. Soon she is outside in the community garden with a green watering can, gloves, flowers, and her neighbor beside her. His line, "Getting your hands dirty is its own adventure!", gently shifts the joke from collecting impressive destinations to noticing that effort, novelty, and pleasure can also exist close to home.

The slower rhythm still contains plenty of doing. Jing and her neighbor work on a wooden bench so other people can sit there in the sun; later she reads with a mug nearby while the orange-and-white cat curls up beside her. The sign behind her says, "THERE'S MORE THAN ONE GOOD LIFE," which matches what the pictures are showing rather than turning quietness into a superior lifestyle. Most importantly, she remains open to invitations: when a friend messages about a small photography show next week, Jing replies, "Yes! I'd love that. Let's go!" She accepts because the invitation genuinely interests her, not because every empty slot needs to become evidence of an exciting life.

The ending brings the idea back to attention. Jing hugs a leafy potted plant by the sunny window and says, "Didn't check in around the world. The world checked in on my windowsill." Her thought, "No post needed. I'll keep this happiness for myself," is not an argument against sharing or traveling; it is a small change in who gets to define the value of the moment. That makes a useful contemporary connection with the supplied line from Chapter 20: Jing stops measuring her weekend by the public rhythm around her and listens more closely to what actually nourishes her. The comic is an imaginative modern reflection on that possibility, not a claim that the ancient sentence has only one fixed lifestyle meaning.
a-weekend-of-your-own.quote: I alone wish to differ from others, and I value being nourished by the Mother.
a-weekend-of-your-own.practice: When your next free day starts filling up, try sorting the plans into two groups: "I genuinely want this" and "I mainly don't want to miss out." Keep what still feels interesting, leave some space, and notice what you naturally choose next. It might be a workshop, a photography show, watering a plant, fixing something useful, or simply reading in the sun.
a-weekend-of-your-own.comicTitle: My Feed Tours the World. I Water the Plants.
a-weekend-of-your-own.comicAlt: Two-page, twelve-panel solarpunk comic set in a lush sunny eco-city. Jing, a young woman in a green jacket with a messy bun, scrolls through posts about skydiving, mountain summits, and gallery visits, then writes an overloaded weekend plan. Surrounded by a backpack, helmet, camera, shoes, and gear, she becomes tired before leaving home. Her friendly neighbor in beige overalls asks whether she truly wants to go or mainly wants people to know she went. Jing cancels most activities but keeps the craft workshop, waters flowers in the community garden, helps repair a wooden bench, reads beside a sleeping orange-and-white cat, and later happily accepts a friend's invitation to a small photography show. In the final panel she hugs a leafy plant by the window and decides the moment does not need to become a social-media post.

trust-built-in-small-things.title: Reliable People Rarely Bring a Soundtrack
trust-built-in-small-things.teaser: One candidate brings verbal fireworks. Another brings a checklist. A small trial task gives the project lead something more useful than a confident first impression.
paragraphs: The opening joke is visual before it becomes verbal. The glasses-wearing project lead sits beside a paper labeled "COMMUNITY CULTURE PROJECT" and a board listing "BETTER EVENTS," "WIDER REACH," and "MORE PARTICIPATION." Candidate A then appears against a rust-red burst, promising connections, channels, and an instant hit, while Candidate B simply says that some things can be done now and others need checking. The page does not declare either personality good or bad; it first places spectacle and clearly stated limits side by side.

The turning point is not a dramatic revelation but a small assignment that begins leaving evidence. The lead chooses Candidate A for the first trial, and A answers confidently, "No problem. Leave it to me!" A few days later, the phone shows messages about "Big moves soon" and "Connecting top-tier resources," but after more days the lead's own follow-ups remain merely sent. The comedy comes from the shrinking distance between enormous language and the very ordinary question on the screen: is there anything concrete to look at yet?

Candidate B changes the texture of the story by putting work on the table. In the upper page, B has already warned that one item may be two days late; later, B opens a laptop showing "DONE 3/5," "TWO TO CONFIRM," "NOTES," and "IMPROVEMENTS." The lead's response, "Now I can actually see progress," names the real shift. The contrast is not charisma versus virtue; it is between claims that are still hard to verify and delivery information that can be inspected, discussed, and updated.

The funniest comparison comes in panel 09, where the two collaboration styles become literal piles. Candidate A's side erupts with "BRILLIANT IDEA!," "CHANGE THE INDUSTRY!," "NEXT BIG THING!," and "RESULTS SOON!," complete with graphic fireworks. Candidate B's side is almost comically plain: "TASKS," "COMPLETED WORK," "TO CONFIRM," and "NEXT STEPS." Sitting between them, the lead observes, "One makes fireworks. One builds steps." The image keeps that line grounded in repeated delivery evidence rather than turning it into a universal judgment about expressive people.

The ending makes the red "RELIABLE" stamp less important than the record behind it. The lead first builds a "DELIVERY LOG" with task, date, risk, and result, then watches what happens over time. Candidate B later hands over the "FINAL VERSION" with content, change notes, assets, and delivery complete all checked, saying the remaining items were finished two days later, exactly as agreed; the handoff gets the wonderfully modest sound effect "CLACK." In the final panel, every delivery-log item is checked and the stamp is being put away. Read alongside Chapter 21, "Its reality is deeply genuine; within it is trust" suggests a limited connection: trust can emerge where words, warnings, timing, and outcomes repeatedly line up in ways that can be checked.
trust-built-in-small-things.quote: Its reality is deeply genuine; within it is trust.
trust-built-in-small-things.practice: In your next collaboration, try delaying the question "Is this person reliable?" Pick one small task instead. Note the promise, deadline, open questions, risks, and actual result. After two or three rounds, look at what consistently became visible, what changed, and whether updates matched the eventual delivery.
trust-built-in-small-things.comicTitle: Reliable People Rarely Bring a Soundtrack
trust-built-in-small-things.comicAlt: Two-page linocut-style comic in black, rust-red, and cream. A glasses-wearing project lead compares Candidate A's energetic promises with Candidate B's concrete updates. Candidate A is shown with verbal fireworks, bold slogans, and unanswered follow-ups; Candidate B presents checklists, risks, a delivery log, and a completed final version two days later as previously stated. The story ends with all four delivery-log items checked, a red "RELIABLE" stamp being put away, and the line "Reliability's soundtrack is the sound of things getting done."

choosing.title: My Bookmarks Have a PhD. I Haven't Started.
choosing.teaser: His saved resources wear graduation caps. His practice notebook is blank. One ten-minute attempt finally gives him something besides an impressive filing system.
paragraphs: The opening turns collecting into a full academic career. The orange-sweater young man sits happily between towers labeled STUDY, INSPIRATION, COURSES, READING, INDUSTRY, TOOLS, and LIFE, while his notebook lies completely blank in the foreground. He confidently says, "Into the Master Learning System it goes," then upgrades the filing ritual with names such as 7-DAY MASTERY, EXPERT SECRETS, ULTIMATE LEARNING, and MENTAL MODELS. Graduation caps perched above the folders make the joke visual before anyone explains it: his resources already look ready for commencement, while he has not yet written a first line.

The comedy escalates because organizing becomes another thing to collect. In panel 03 he thinks, "I'll start practicing once I've organized the methods," while the notebook itself answers silently with "STILL BLANK." Then a tablet offers ORGANIZE YOUR COLLECTION, promising a path "FROM CHAOS TO A SYSTEM" with SORT, MAINTAIN, and USE YOUR KNOWLEDGE beside a bright BUY NOW button. His delighted reaction, "Finish this and I'll be complete!", captures the loop perfectly: preparation for action has produced yet another purchasable layer of preparation.

The blue-shirted, short-haired woman supplies the turning point without changing the room or removing any folders. She points directly at the empty practice book and says, "The practice book's still empty. Your folders have more degrees than you." Beside them, the tower now literally climbs through ELEMENTARY TO-READ, DIPLOMA INSPIRATION, BACHELOR'S RESOURCES, MASTER'S COURSES, and PhD BOOKMARKS, complete with a graduation cap. The young man looks up at this absurd academic monument and admits, "...Accurate. Have I majored in Getting Ready to Start?" The joke works because the diagnosis is already sitting on the desk in plain sight.

The lower page changes the sequence of actions rather than staging a dramatic purge. He says, "No more life upgrades in the cart today," closes the purchase page, and reaches for a PRACTICAL ACTION GUIDE already beside him. Next he sets a visible 10:00 timer and writes in the notebook. His first diagram is rough, surrounded by arrows, boxes, and crumpled paper, but the woman smiles as he jokes, "Crooked—but at least there's finally something to be crooked!" When he reaches a genuinely uncertain step, he consults the guide and writes "REVISE USING THE ANSWER," using information to solve a live problem instead of postponing practice until everything is organized.

By panel 11, the difference is small but concrete: the dated page shows checks beside DRAW THE STRUCTURE, LIST KEY POINTS, and WRITE NEXT STEP, while KEEP PRACTICING remains unfinished. His line, "Ten minutes. Finally, not ten new bookmarks," makes the scale of the victory part of the joke. In the final panel, the towering PhD BOOKMARKS and other degree-labeled folders are still there; nothing has been magically simplified. He and the woman simply sit with their mugs, the worked notebook open in front of them, as he says, "The resources are sky-high. I'll start on the ground." Read alongside "With less, one gains; with more, one becomes confused," the comic offers one contemporary reflection: when options multiply, choosing one sufficient resource and acting on it can make the next step easier to see. It is not presented as the only possible meaning of the ancient line.
choosing.quote: With less, one gains; with more, one becomes confused.
choosing.practice: You might choose just one saved resource that is useful enough for today, set a ten-minute timer, and make one small attempt. Mark anything you genuinely do not know, then look it up only when that question appears. The goal is not to organize the whole archive first, but simply to leave one real trace of practice on the page.
choosing.comicTitle: My Bookmarks Have a PhD. I Haven't Started.
choosing.comicAlt: A twelve-panel warm hand-painted comic shows an orange-sweater young man surrounded by colorful folders, books, tablets, notebooks, mugs, and graduation caps. He first keeps naming and organizing saved learning resources while his practice notebook stays blank. A short-haired woman in a blue shirt points out that his folders have more degrees than he does. He closes a course-purchase screen, opens a practical action guide, sets a ten-minute timer, draws an imperfect diagram, checks a specific answer when stuck, and completes several small practice steps. In the ending, the giant degree-labeled folder tower remains, but the notebook is finally filled with work as the two characters smile over their mugs.

a-pace-after-enthusiasm.title: My Enthusiasm Finished a Marathon. I'm Still Tying My Shoes.
a-pace-after-enthusiasm.teaser: His enthusiasm buys all the running gear. His legs file a complaint the next day. A smaller plan—and a smartwatch suggesting rest—help him find a pace he wants to return to.
paragraphs: The opening joke is built from visible excess. In the running shop, the curly-haired man in blue proudly holds up a shoe while the table in front of him is crowded with footwear, bottles, a cap, bags, and other training gear. His friend in orange cheers him on, and the whole scene feels less like buying one pair of shoes than launching a new identity. The next panel immediately pushes that enthusiasm too far: he is sweating along the riverside while thinking, "Ten kilometers on day one! Amazing! I can do this!" The comic does not present that distance as sensible beginner advice. Its humor comes from showing how quickly excitement has turned into an oversized first attempt.

The next day supplies the physical punchline. On the stairs, the man is hunched over, gripping the railing, with little wavy marks around his legs and the caption "NEXT DAY." His line, "Oh... my legs... whose legs are these?" turns yesterday's confidence into a very ordinary comic complaint. On the sofa, however, he makes a second leap: from one overdone run to "Maybe I've got no discipline." His friend does not answer with a heroic training speech. She points out that it is only day two, and the conversation later reframes the problem more gently: not every day has to feel like a launch event.

The turning point becomes visible when they stop treating running as all-or-nothing. First, the two simply walk beside the river, chatting in the same blue and orange sportswear, and the man admits that it feels less exhausting. Then he sits down with a pen and makes a notebook plan. The page visibly includes "RUN 3 km," "WALK 2 km," "REST 1 DAY," "ADJUST TO HOW I FEEL," and "ENJOY IT." These distances belong to the character's example rather than a universal prescription. What matters in the story is the change in structure: effort, walking, rest, and adjustment are now all allowed to belong to the same plan.

The later panels test that new idea instead of merely stating it. On a day when he has no energy, the man sits slumped on a park bench and worries that skipping a run means he is quitting again. His friend, holding a bottle beside him, answers that they can walk and that it does not have to be all or nothing. Soon afterward, the two are running by the river again, but his line has changed completely: "Two kilometers today. Just right! Not drained. I'd come back." The joke is quieter here, but the visual contrast is strong: the earlier runner tried to solve the future in one exhausting burst, while this version finishes with enough willingness left to imagine returning.

The final joke belongs to the smartwatch. Earlier it is part of the man's serious running equipment; now he stares at its screen and laughs because it says "REST SUGGESTED / RECOVER WELL." He says he used to treat the watch like a supervisor, while his friend observes that even the data can remind him to take a break. The last panel deliberately leaves the running path behind. He is reclining comfortably on the sofa with his hands behind his head, while his friend sits nearby holding a mug, and he says the watch feels more like a friend now. The supplied line from the Daodejing observes that intense forces do not last indefinitely. The comic uses that idea loosely, not as a running manual, but as a way to question the habit of making every beginning maximally intense.
a-pace-after-enthusiasm.quote: A fierce wind does not last through the morning; a downpour does not last through the day.
a-pace-after-enthusiasm.practice: If there is something you tend to begin at maximum intensity, try making the next round a little smaller. Do one shorter session, remove one optional demand, or put a rest day directly into the plan. Then notice which pace makes it easier to say, a few days later, "I'd come back."
a-pace-after-enthusiasm.comicTitle: My Enthusiasm Finished a Marathon. I'm Still Tying My Shoes.
a-pace-after-enthusiasm.comicAlt: A warm six-panel-per-page 3D animated comic follows a curly-haired man in blue sportswear and his woman friend in orange sportswear. He buys abundant running gear, attempts ten kilometers on his first day, struggles on stairs the next day, collapses on a sofa, then learns to walk, rest, and make a flexible notebook plan. On the second page he walks with his friend, adjusts his plan, rests on a bench when low on energy, enjoys a shorter two-kilometer run, laughs when his smartwatch displays "REST SUGGESTED / RECOVER WELL," and finally relaxes on the sofa while his friend holds a mug.

stop-standing-on-tiptoe.title: Fast to Say Yes. Slow to Be Seen Again.
stop-standing-on-tiptoe.teaser: Every effortless yes lifts Neng higher on a pair of absurd stilts. Three deadlines on the same day bring him back to earth—and to a plan he can actually deliver.
paragraphs: The opening joke is built around repetition. The dark-suited manager asks Neng to take a proposal, the green-shirted colleague adds next week's event, then data analysis and an urgent request arrive in quick succession. Neng answers almost every bubble with some version of "No problem!" and even throws in an enthusiastic "Me!" The comic then turns that verbal confidence into a visual object: labeled stacks for PROPOSAL, EVENT, DATA, URGENT REQUEST, and OTHER TASKS rise around him while his feet are placed on long wooden stilts. His smile disappears as the stilts grow taller. The angular buildings, flying papers, and tilted perspective make the gag clear without needing an abstract lecture: every effortless yes adds another layer beneath someone who is already trying to balance.

The conflict becomes concrete in the deadline panel. A huge sheet marked DEADLINES shows PROPOSAL, EVENT LAUNCH, and DATA REPORT all circled for APR 12. Neng grabs his head, eyes wide, and asks, "Three deadlines... same day?!" The comedy comes from how late the obvious arithmetic reaches him. In the next panel, his colleague asks how the tasks are going while he is still stranded high on the stilts. His answer stretches into "Soon! Doing them! Soon! Sooo..." That elongated "Sooo..." is the visual and verbal punch line: he still sounds as though delivery is just around the corner, but the picture shows someone physically separated from a normal working height by the commitments he has accumulated.

The lower page does not solve the problem by magically removing the workload. In panel 07, the green-shirted colleague reaches upward and tells Neng, "You're high enough. Come down first," while he nervously replies, "Ah! I'll... try..." Once he is back at the desk, they make the work visible instead of leaving it as one intimidating tower. The same categories are stacked beside them—PROPOSAL, EVENT, DATA REPORT, URGENT REQUEST, OTHER TASKS—and Neng finally asks how many things he actually agreed to. The turning point is practical rather than heroic: they look at the commitments, notice the three APR 12 deadlines again, and replace vague confidence with a list that can be discussed.

Panel 10 shows the most important change through a physical prop: a board titled NEW PLAN. The proposal stays on APR 12, the event moves to APR 19, the data work becomes a CORE VERSION due APR 12, and EXTRA REQUEST DEFERRED is left unchecked. His colleague proposes renegotiating, while Neng answers, "Be clear about capacity. Stop saying yes to everything." The idea is tested immediately in panel 11 when the manager brings another urgent request. This time Neng does not repeat "No problem!" He says, "Let me check my schedule," explains that he cannot take it now, and offers to assess it next week and provide a clear date. The change is small, specific, and visible in his words.

The ending deliberately brings Neng back to an ordinary height. In panel 12 he is seated at a normal desk among laptops and papers, smiling with one hand behind his head as he says, "Less superhuman today. Finally delivering something." His colleague answers, "That's good!" Work has not vanished; the joke has simply stopped requiring stilts. The closing line makes the visual metaphor explicit: saying yes too fast puts you on stilts, while slowing down and speaking clearly helps you stand steadier. Read alongside the supplied excerpt, the connection is limited rather than literal: the comic is not illustrating an ancient scene, but it does play with the image of standing and not standing securely. Its office version asks what happens when appearing capable lifts you higher than your actual capacity can support.
stop-standing-on-tiptoe.quote: One who stands on tiptoe does not stand firm.
stop-standing-on-tiptoe.practice: The next time an unexpected task arrives, you might borrow Neng's second-page move instead of his first-page reflex. Before saying "No problem," name the two or three commitments already taking most of your time, check the dates, and offer one realistic option: a later deadline, a smaller core version, or a specific time when you can assess the request.
stop-standing-on-tiptoe.comicTitle: Fast to Say Yes. Slow to Be Seen Again.
stop-standing-on-tiptoe.comicAlt: Two-page, twelve-panel Expressionist office comic in angular blue, red, yellow, and cream brushwork. Neng, a black-haired man in a white shirt, repeatedly says "No problem!" as a glasses-wearing manager and a green-shirted female colleague add proposal, event, data, urgent, and other tasks. The work becomes towering paper stacks and Neng rises on long wooden stilts. Three deadlines all land on APR 12, leaving him panicked and promising "Soon!" His colleague helps him come down, list the work, and create a NEW PLAN with revised dates, a core data version, and a deferred extra request. When the manager brings another urgent task, Neng checks his schedule instead of instantly agreeing. The final panel shows him relaxed at a normal desk, finally delivering something while his colleague smiles.

a-method-that-fits-your-day.title: His Dawn Routine Sent Me Back to Bed
a-method-that-fits-your-day.teaser: She copies a five-o’clock routine—just when her own workday ends. A row of coffee mugs and an accidental desk nap help her learn to borrow the method, not the clock.
paragraphs: The opening joke is built around a very specific misunderstanding. On her phone, the curly-haired man in the cream hoodie appears against a bright sunrise with the message, "UP AT FIVE! READ, EXERCISE, WORK. A FULL LIFE!" and the poster beneath him promises, "EARLY MORNINGS, MORE FREEDOM." Sitting in her navy pajamas, the woman looks genuinely inspired and says, "So disciplined! I'll try!" She immediately sets her phone to 05:00, complete with "ALARM" and "A BETTER YOU." The black-and-white cat is already lounging nearby, which makes the enthusiasm feel even funnier: she is treating one attractive schedule as if the useful idea and the exact clock time must come as a package.

Panel 03 reveals the missing piece. At 05:00 AM the alarm explodes into "RING RING," but instead of beginning a heroic morning, the woman reaches out from under the floral quilt and says, "Oh... I only just finished work!" The next panel turns that mismatch into a visual gag. She sits at her laptop looking exhausted, gripping another floral mug while several more cups crowd the desk like evidence of an increasingly complicated plan. Behind her, the wall still declares "EARLY = SUCCESS." Nothing in the comic says early rising itself is wrong; the humor comes from watching a slogan remain perfectly confident while her actual work schedule makes that borrowed timetable absurd.

By 10:00 AM, the cream-hoodie man arrives cheerfully with "Let's see how it's going!" only to find her asleep at the desk beside the laptop, mugs, papers, and the unbothered cat. The key joke lands in the next panel when he explains, "I start at five. You shut down at five. Different time zones!" Her floating question mark makes the realization visible before the second page spells it out. During "TALKING ROUTINES" he describes what five o'clock means in his own day—"Run, read, work. Works for me!"—and in "THE CATCH" she finally answers, "Ah! You start your day when I finish work!" The problem was never a lack of effort; they had been using the same number on the clock to describe opposite ends of their days.

The turning point is practical rather than dramatic. In "ADJUST," the woman sits back at her desk with a pen, laptop, floral mug, and a new written plan. Her sentence, "Borrow the method, not the clock. I'll study after I've slept," keeps the useful part of the experiment while dropping the copied timing. The checklist makes that change concrete: "STUDY AFTER SLEEP," "KEEP USEFUL METHODS," "DON'T COPY BLINDLY," "MY OWN RHYTHM," and "ADJUST GRADUALLY." Even the stacked books—"DESIGN," "ENGLISH," "IDEAS," and "LIFE"—show that her interests and intentions have not disappeared. She is not abandoning study; she is rearranging when it happens. The next panel, "REST FIRST," simply shows her asleep under the quilt with the cat nearby and the thought, "First, some real sleep. Try a new rhythm tomorrow."

The ending quietly shows what that adjustment looks like. In "AFTERNOON PRACTICE," she is upright at the desk, writing beside her laptop, pencil cup, floral mug, sleeping cat, and books labeled "DESIGN PRACTICE," "ENGLISH," and "IDEAS." She says, "After sleep, studying feels better. I'm more alert!" The final panel relaxes even further: she leans back with the cat stretched across the desk, the city glowing outside, and says, "A method needs to fit. A fancy size label isn't enough." The closing line—"The rhythm that fits you is a good place to start."—connects naturally with Chapter 25's image of following larger conditions rather than forcing an abstract template onto reality. That is one contemporary reflection on the passage, not a claim that the ancient text prescribes a particular sleep schedule.
a-method-that-fits-your-day.quote: People follow Earth; Earth follows Heaven; Heaven follows the Dao; the Dao follows what is naturally so.
a-method-that-fits-your-day.practice: If you are copying a routine that works well for someone else, try separating the useful method from its exact clock time. You might keep one small element—such as a regular study block—but place it after you have slept and at a time that fits your own workday. Try that version for a few days, notice how workable it feels, and adjust without turning the alarm itself into a test of discipline.
a-method-that-fits-your-day.comicTitle: His Dawn Routine Sent Me Back to Bed
a-method-that-fits-your-day.comicAlt: Two-page, twelve-panel folk-art comic with floral, bird, tiger, and cloud motifs. A woman in navy pajamas admires a curly-haired man in a cream hoodie who promotes a 5:00 AM routine, so she sets a 05:00 alarm. The alarm rings just after she has finished work, and she struggles at her laptop behind a growing row of floral coffee mugs before falling asleep at the desk. The man later explains that he starts his day at five while she shuts down at five. She writes a new plan to borrow the method rather than the clock, sleeps first beside a black-and-white cat, studies in the afternoon, and ends relaxed at her desk with the message that a method needs to fit.

before-sending-the-angry-message.title: This Message Almost Resigned for Me
before-sending-the-angry-message.teaser: An angry reply nearly reaches Send. A glass of water, a short walk, and three note cards help its author make her point without letting anger write the ending.
paragraphs: The opening makes the frustration visible before the woman even starts typing. In panel 01, the short-haired woman in a red sweater grips a WORK REVIEW marked "AVERAGE," "LACKS INITIATIVE," and "COMMUNICATION NEEDS IMPROVEMENT" while the black, red, and gold office around her seems almost as angular as her expression. By panel 02 she is at the laptop declaring, "I'm writing back! Enough!" with an email addressed to her manager. Nothing suggests resignation has actually happened; the comedy comes from how quickly an upsetting review is turning into a reply large enough to feel career-sized.

Panels 03 and 04 push that impulse into visual exaggeration. The woman announces, "Done! Every sentence is how I really feel!" while smoky, jagged words erupt beside the laptop: "UNPROFESSIONAL!", "UNFAIR!", "YOU DON'T UNDERSTAND!", and "I'VE HAD ENOUGH!" Then the page cuts to a close-up of her finger hovering over a bright red SEND button as she says, "Send it! Right now!" The finger never presses it. That unpressed button is the first important fact of the story: the anger is real, but the message is still under her control.

The turning point arrives through an ordinary prop rather than a grand speech. Her long-haired friend in a gray sweater appears with a glass of water and says, "Wait. Have some water." The next line supplies the warmest joke on the first page: "Your punctuation wants a fight more than your message does." The woman does not suddenly become cheerful or decide the review was fair. In panel 06 she is still slumped beside the laptop and admits, "Maybe I really am too angry. I just feel so wronged." The change is smaller and more believable: she recognizes the feeling before letting it choose the next action.

The second page turns that pause into visible editing work. Panel 07 shows the reply labeled "DRAFT / SAVE FOR NOW," and panel 08 sends the woman outside for "A little air" and "Another angle." Back at the table, her friend proposes, "Let's separate the parts," beside three cards labeled "FACTS / WHAT HAPPENED," "REQUEST / WHAT I WANT," and "ATTACKS / LEAVE OUT." The categories are slightly funny because they make an emotional explosion look like office stationery, but that is exactly the point of the scene: what was one furious mass can now be sorted into material she wants to communicate and material she does not want to send.

The ending deliberately stops short of a tidy victory. In panel 10 the woman writes a "NEW REPLY - DRAFT" organized as "WHAT HAPPENED," "MY UNDERSTANDING," "REQUEST," and "NEXT STEPS." Her friend jokes, "Better! A professional, not a volcano," and the woman answers that they still need to talk, but "At least anger didn't press Send for me." The final panel keeps the issue unresolved: she rests at the desk with a black-and-white cat, the water glass still nearby, and a sunset outside while saying she is readier to discuss the problem and will sleep first. The supplied line from the Daodejing can be connected to this only as a contemporary reflection: steadiness can give restless action a base. The comic does not say anger is wrong or that conflict should be swallowed; it shows someone making enough room between feeling and action to state the facts and her request more clearly.
before-sending-the-angry-message.quote: The heavy is the root of the light; stillness is the master of restlessness.
before-sending-the-angry-message.practice: If you have a message you urgently want to send, you could first leave it as a draft and step away from the screen for a few minutes. When you return, try marking its parts as "facts," "request," and "attacks," then decide which parts actually need to travel with the message.
before-sending-the-angry-message.comicTitle: This Message Almost Resigned for Me
before-sending-the-angry-message.comicAlt: A two-page, twelve-panel German Expressionist-style comic in rough black, red, and gold woodcut textures. A short-black-haired woman in a red sweater receives a negative work review, angrily drafts an email to her manager, and hovers over a red SEND button without pressing it. Her long-dark-haired friend in a gray sweater brings a glass of water and jokes that the punctuation wants a fight. The woman admits she is angry and feels wronged, saves the email as a draft, takes a walk through an angular city street, and returns to sort the response into note cards for facts, requests, and attacks to leave out. She rewrites the reply as a draft organized around what happened, her understanding, her request, and next steps. The friend jokes that she now looks like a professional rather than a volcano. In the last panel, the unresolved issue remains, but the woman rests beside a black-and-white cat, a water glass, her laptop, and a sunset, deciding to sleep before discussing it.

find-another-use.title: This Mug Found a Better Job After Retirement
find-another-use.teaser: A chipped mug puts on a tie and interviews for a new job. Drinking is out; after a careful check, its next career turns out to involve pencils instead of coffee.
paragraphs: The opening joke treats an ordinary damaged mug like the hero of a very serious workplace drama. A curly-haired man in a green sweater and blue apron studies the chipped floral mug and wonders whether loving it means he has to keep it. One panel later, the mug has grown arms and legs, put on a blue tie, packed a brown suitcase marked "JOB SEEKER," and marched off to interview for another position. The framed slogan "MORE THAN ONE ROLE IN LIFE" makes the career-change metaphor even more solemn, which is exactly what makes the scene funny.

The drinking-job interview does not bend the rules for sentiment. A tall glass wearing spectacles sits behind the desk beneath a "DRINKING JOB INTERVIEW" sign and calmly explains that the damaged rim is not safe for drinking. The mug answers, "I understand..." and later walks away with its suitcase, asking whether losing that one role means becoming useless. The next visual turn answers the question through props rather than a lecture: a little plant and a cheerful penpot appear as alternative possibilities, each with its own tiny sign, so the story opens new uses without pretending the original use is still suitable.

Before the mug actually changes jobs, the comic returns from personified comedy to practical inspection. The man holds the chipped rim close, checks the damage, sharp edges, cracks, and suitable use, and explicitly says that it is no longer safe for drinking. On the lower page he repeats that careful examination with a written checklist. This pause matters because the story does not jump from affection directly to repair. The visible turning point is assessment: first decide what the object can safely do now, then decide whether a new role makes sense.

The new role is presented as one option among several, not as a command to rescue everything. Three doors offer "PLANT INTERN," "PEN DESIGNER," and "SMALL-ITEM STORAGE," while the mug happily announces that other jobs might fit. The man then carefully removes sharp edges and states again, "No more drinking. A pen holder might fit." In the next panel, separate broken pieces go into a box labeled "DISPOSE RESPONSIBLY," beside the sign "KEEP WHAT FITS / LET THE REST GO." The humour stays gentle because the comic allows both outcomes: some things can be repurposed, while others can simply be released.

The ending gives the mug a visible, specific second career. It stands on the desk full of pencils and brushes, still proudly wearing its tie, with books titled "IDEAS," "DESIGN," and "LIFE" beside it. In the final panel, the man rests his cheek on one hand and looks at the pen-filled mug near a sketchbook, lamp, and green plant, saying, "Successful transfer. Farther from lips. Closer to inspiration." The closing line, "An ending can make room for a more suitable beginning," connects naturally with the supplied passage as a contemporary reflection: not discarding something too quickly can reveal another fitting use, while the comic also keeps safety checks and responsible disposal firmly in view.
find-another-use.quote: No material is cast aside; this is called hidden illumination.
find-another-use.practice: The next time you have a damaged object you still like, try the same three-part check shown in the comic: is it safe, can its original use continue, and is there a suitable non-food-contact use instead? If nothing fits, letting it go responsibly is also a valid ending. If a safer new role does fit, give it a place that matches what it can do now.
find-another-use.comicTitle: This Mug Found a Better Job After Retirement
find-another-use.comicAlt: A twelve-panel Arts and Crafts-style comic with botanical borders follows a curly brown-haired man in a green sweater and blue apron and an anthropomorphic chipped floral mug. The mug wears a blue tie, carries a suitcase, interviews with a bespectacled glass for a drinking job, considers plant, pen, and storage roles, undergoes damage and sharp-edge checks, retires permanently from drinking use, and finally becomes a pen holder on the man's desk while unrelated broken pieces are placed in a box labeled "DISPOSE RESPONSIBLY."

resolve-without-an-extra-blow.title: Problem Solved. My Mouth Is Still Working Overtime.
resolve-without-an-extra-blow.teaser: The office problem is solved. His imaginary victory cannon still wants one more shot. An empty message box turns out to be the best final word.
paragraphs: The opening stays firmly in the real office. The blue-shirted man points at the equipment layout and argues that the current position blocks cables, hurts ventilation, narrows the aisle, and makes maintenance awkward. The woman in the red blazer first answers, "It's always been there. Seemed fine," then takes another look. By panel 03 she agrees that the equipment should be moved, and he answers with a cheerful thumbs-up and "Agreed!" The practical disagreement is already over; that is exactly why his lingering victory expression becomes funny.

Panels 04 and 05 turn the unnecessary extra sentence into a deliberately ridiculous fantasy. The man imagines thinking, "Should've listened to me in the first place!" while an enormous cartoon cannon fires an "I TOLD YOU SO" projectile. The next image exaggerates the social cost: the blast smashes a wooden bridge whose two sides are labeled "UNDERSTANDING" and "TRUST," accompanied by a huge "CRACK!" Nothing physical happens to the coworkers; the cannon and bridge are clearly visual metaphors for what a triumphant aftershot could do to the cooperation they have just repaired.

The second page shows that the temptation has not vanished. In panel 07, the man's fantasy self appears in sunglasses beside a labeled "VICTORY CANNON," happily repeating "Should've listened to me!" But panel 08 supplies the turning point from inside his own thought process: "No. Say that and the bridge we just fixed cracks again." The broken bridge reappears, so the joke becomes a choice rather than merely a warning. He can enjoy the private fantasy without converting it into another round of the argument.

A tiny office sound finally pulls the scene completely back to reality. In panel 09, the older coworker with glasses looks over from behind his computer and says only, "Ahem..." The blue-shirted man freezes with his hand near his mouth, yellow surprise marks beside his head, while the woman in red turns toward him with a question mark. Instead of adding the victory line, he redirects his energy into the next concrete step. At the monitor he explains, "Tower here, monitor by the window, cables this way. More room for airflow and access," and she replies, "Agreed. Let's do that."

The ending makes the change physical and pleasantly ordinary. The two coworkers lift the equipment together as he counts, "Together. One, two, three!" and she answers, "Got it!" In the final panel they are relaxed and smiling, and the large message box in front of him remains completely empty. His last thought, "The job's done. My mouth can clock off too," lands the joke without requiring another speech. Read beside Chapter 30, the comic suggests a limited contemporary connection: once a practical aim has been achieved, there may be no need to turn the result into leverage over another person. That does not mean withholding useful disagreement; the comic shows the man stating his case clearly. The restraint begins only after the problem has already been solved.
resolve-without-an-extra-blow.quote: One who is good achieves the result and stops there; do not use it as a means to impose force.
resolve-without-an-extra-blow.practice: The next time an issue has just been settled, notice the sentence you are about to add. Is it helping with the next step, or only giving the victory cannon one more shot? If it is the second, you might leave the message box empty and move on to the work you have already agreed to do.
resolve-without-an-extra-blow.comicTitle: Problem Solved. My Mouth Is Still Working Overtime.
resolve-without-an-extra-blow.comicAlt: A twelve-panel American comic-book-style office story with bright blue, yellow, and red halftones. A black-haired man in a blue shirt and a brunette woman in a red blazer debate computer equipment placement, then agree on a better layout. The man's imagined "I TOLD YOU SO" victory cannon blasts apart a metaphorical bridge labeled "UNDERSTANDING" and "TRUST." An older coworker's quiet "Ahem..." interrupts the fantasy. The pair then plan the layout, lift the equipment together, and finish smiling. In the final panel, an empty unsent message box sits in front of the man as he thinks that his mouth can clock off too.

after-winning-an-argument.title: I Won the Argument. Home Sounds Like Someone Moved Out.
after-winning-an-argument.teaser: Sheng brings ten items of chore evidence and imagines an award ceremony. The cold dinner afterward raises a less convenient question: did winning make home any better?
paragraphs: The opening joke is wonderfully concrete: Sheng is not merely arguing about chores; he is presenting a case. At the kitchen table, his partner sits with folded arms as they argue over whose work goes unnoticed, and in the next panel he produces a spiral notebook headed "CHORE EVIDENCE (10)." Trash, dishes, laundry, floors, cat litter, groceries, cooking, repairs, tidying, errands—the ordinary mess of shared life has suddenly become courtroom material. Both people look tired, but instead of comparing what each needs, they begin comparing who has suffered more. The comedy comes from watching a home conversation acquire the seriousness of a project review.

Panel 03 pushes Sheng's sense of victory into full fantasy. He appears in a tuxedo under spotlights, trophy raised above his head, while "CHORE CONTRIBUTOR OF THE YEAR" and "HOUSEWORK COUNTS TOO" decorate an imaginary awards stage. The grandeur lasts exactly one panel. Back in the real dining room, the food is cold, the couple sit far apart, and both speech balloons contain only dots. That cut from applause to silence is the page's sharpest visual turn: the argument may have produced a winner, but the actual room has become less comfortable for both people.

The turning point comes through the friend in the olive shirt and glasses. At the café, with mugs on the table and "GOOD COFFEE / GOOD FRIENDS / TALK" behind them, he asks whether winning made things better for the couple. Sheng first admits that it did not; on the next page he answers even more plainly, "No. More tiring, actually." He then goes home and begins somewhere different: not with another list, but with an apology for the hurtful things he said and for being so focused on proving himself right. His partner does not instantly erase the conflict either; she says she was upset too and asks whether they can talk properly.

Their next conversation stays deliberately practical. Sheng says work follows him home and offers to take more cooking and trash; his partner names childcare, errands, tidying, dishes, and cleaning. Two notebooks make those loads visible without pretending they are mathematically equivalent, and the whiteboard in the following panel turns the conversation into a trial arrangement: cooking three times a week, trash, after-dinner dishes, weekend cleanup, childcare and runs, tidying, floors, groceries. Crucially, they describe it as something to try and adjust. The comic does not claim that a chore chart fixes a relationship; it shows two people replacing a contest with a workable next experiment.

The ending brings the earlier trophy joke back down to household scale. Sheng and his partner wash dishes side by side, the mood visibly lighter, and then Sheng holds up an ordinary yellow sponge with mock ceremony. "This finally has a practical use," he says, and she laughs that it is actually being put to work this time. The supplied line, "When victory is won, treat it with funeral rites," is not a literal description of the scene, but it offers a useful lens for it: some victories deserve restraint rather than celebration, especially when defeating the other person leaves the shared life colder. Here, the comic's final image replaces symbolic triumph with a sponge, a sink, and two people doing the work together.
after-winning-an-argument.quote: When victory is won, treat it with funeral rites.
