after-winning-an-argument.practice: In the next argument, try setting aside "who is more right" for a moment. Each person can name one specific thing that has been exhausting lately, then choose one small responsibility that could be redistributed or tested differently. The goal does not have to be instant harmony; it can simply be making the next ordinary evening a little easier to share.
after-winning-an-argument.comicTitle: I Won the Argument. Home Sounds Like Someone Moved Out.
after-winning-an-argument.comicAlt: Two-page, twelve-panel painted graphic novel about Sheng and his partner arguing over household chores. Sheng presents a ten-item chore notebook, imagines himself receiving a trophy for being the household's greatest contributor, then returns to a cold, silent dinner where the couple sit far apart. A bespectacled friend asks whether winning actually improved things, prompting Sheng to admit it made home more tiring and quiet. Back home, Sheng apologizes, the couple discuss their separate loads using notebooks, and they write a trial chore split on a whiteboard. The final panels show them washing dishes together before Sheng jokingly holds up a yellow kitchen sponge as something finally put to practical use, making his partner laugh.

comparing.title: Someone Got Promoted. Even My Plant Is Anxious.
comparing.teaser: A classmate gets promoted. Bi starts measuring his plant against everyone else’s milestones. Its roots—and a pot labeled “No IPO”—help him reconsider the ruler.
paragraphs: The opening joke is wonderfully literal. Bi slumps over his phone while a classmate's feed announces a promotion, a new home, and a new start. Beside him, books labeled "PROMOTION," "HOME," "MARRIAGE," and "MILESTONES" make the comparison feel as if an entire life checklist has been stacked on his desk. His attention then lands on the tiny potted seedling, and the anxiety spreads by association: he tells it that everyone else is flowering while it barely has a sprout, with "HURRY UP, GROW!" stuck to the pot. The plant has done nothing wrong, which is exactly why the scene is funny.

Bi makes the comparison even more concrete in panel 03 by bringing out an actual ruler. Around it are labels for "CLASSMATE: PROMOTED," "COLLEAGUE: HOUSE," "FRIEND: MARRIED," and "OTHERS: STARTUP," while his own position is reduced to "ME: ?" The woman in mustard overalls catches him doing this and asks whether he is comparing progress with the plant again. Her interruption matters because she does not argue that the other milestones are unimportant; she points out that Bi has turned other people's events into the measuring marks for his own life. His embarrassed "Huh? I was just..." keeps the exchange playful rather than preachy.

The turning point arrives through specific evidence rather than reassurance alone. The woman asks what Bi has done in the past six months, and the notebook titled "MY SIX MONTHS" lists learning to cook, keeping moving, reading three books, caring for family, changing work direction, and still showing up. Bi answers, "More than I thought." In the next panel she holds a watering can beside an enlarged view of a plant with a dense web of roots exposed beneath the soil. His surprised response—"Wow. So much happening underneath!"—works visually because the comic does not pretend the small seedling suddenly became the larger plant. Instead, the separate rooted plant makes hidden development visible without claiming that every life or every plant follows the same timetable.

Bi then changes what he records. In "MY PROGRESS," he writes down focused work, cooking a meal, talking with family, repotting the plant, having a steadier week, and taking one step toward his direction. The following illustration keeps the contrast rather than erasing it: under "THEIR PACE" stands a large established tree accompanied by promotion, house, marriage, and startup, while "MY PACE" contains a much smaller seedling with its own roots. Bi asks, "Different seeds, different seasons. Why one ruler?" and follows it with "I have my own rhythm." The ruler has stopped being the judge even though the visible difference in size remains.

The ending becomes quieter instead of turning into a victory montage. Over botanical mugs, the woman tells Bi that slower is okay and that he is living and growing; he replies that he would like to care for what is here now. In the final panel the original pot still contains only a small shoot, and an orange-and-white cat sleeps peacefully beside it. The pot's label—"NO IPO. STILL GROWING."—delivers the last joke, while Bi echoes it: "One leaf so far. No IPO. Still growing. Me too." The closing line, "Some flowers catch your eye early. Some are putting down roots," connects naturally with the supplied Daodejing passage as a contemporary reflection: attention shifts away from defeating someone else's timeline and toward recognizing and directing one's own life.
comparing.quote: One who overcomes others has strength; one who overcomes oneself is strong.
comparing.practice: On a blank page, leave other people's milestones off the ruler for a moment. Write down three to five things from the past six months that you actually learned, cared for, changed, sustained, or moved toward. They do not need to look impressive. The exercise is simply to notice what may already be taking root below the most visible outcomes.
comparing.comicTitle: Someone Got Promoted. Even My Plant Is Anxious.
comparing.comicAlt: Two-page botanical watercolor comic in twelve panels. Bi, a dark-haired young man in a green shirt, becomes anxious after seeing a classmate's promotion and new home, compares himself with milestones and even measures a tiny seedling with a ruler. A woman in mustard overalls helps him review a six-month checklist and shows him the dense roots of a larger plant. Bi begins recording everyday progress, contrasts "THEIR PACE" with "MY PACE," and ends beside the original small seedling and a sleeping orange-and-white cat. The pot reads "NO IPO. STILL GROWING."

help-without-becoming-indispensable.title: I Became the Office's Only Remote Control
help-without-becoming-indispensable.teaser: Kong is the office’s only remote control—even lunch needs his approval. A shared decision guide finally lets the team work and him take a bathroom break.
paragraphs: The opening joke is wonderfully literal. Kong, in his bright red jacket, sits at his laptop while the gray-blazer woman and the glasses-wearing man crowd in from both sides with questions: "Kong, which proposal?", "Kong, send this?", and "Kong, are these numbers right?" The composition makes him look less like a colleague than the single control panel for the whole office. Panel 02 pushes the gag into lunch: Kong already has noodles hanging from his chopsticks, yet one coworker needs help answering a client and the other wants a budget checked. His reply, "Two bites. I'll check!", is funny because even a mouthful of noodles has become a tiny scheduling window. The wall slogan "EFFICIENCY NEEDS DIRECTION" adds an ironic backdrop to an office where all direction currently comes from one person.

The first real turn comes when Kong takes half a day off for an appointment. In panel 03 he walks away with a backpack under the wall message "HEALTH MATTERS TOO", thinking, "Half a day should be fine?" Panel 04 immediately answers him: his phone fills with a TEAM CHAT (12) stream asking how to handle something, reporting that a client asked again, requesting a version choice, and finally calling "Online? Urgent! @Kong." The visual joke is that Kong has barely left before the office seems to lose its operating system. His thought, "Half a day and everything stops?", mixes alarm with a strange sense of importance. That feeling peaks in panel 05, where he leans back beneath "ONE PERSON IS A FORCE" and thinks, "They can't do without me. I keep everyone secure."

Panel 06 punctures that flattering interpretation. The woman asks whether Kong can still take tomorrow off, while the glasses-wearing man says, "We need you in a meeting. Who else decides?" Between them stands a black silhouette marked with a question mark, turning the missing backup into a visual character of its own. Kong's thought — "Need a body double just to take leave?" — makes the cost of being indispensable concrete. The lower page does not solve this by having Kong simply refuse to help. Instead, panel 07 shows him at a board writing a shared decision guide with three headings: "CRITERIA", "AUTHORITY", and "WHEN TO ASK." His coworkers react positively, and the joke quietly changes direction: the office's human remote control starts documenting what the buttons actually do.

The guide becomes more specific in panel 08. Under "CLIENT QUESTIONS", the team is asked whether an issue is repeated, whether the risk is manageable, and whether it is within budget; the authorized side lists "UP TO RMB500", "ROUTINE DEADLINES", and "ESCALATE UNCERTAINTY." The woman captures the new logic with, "Guide first, not you first?" and Kong answers, "Yes. Assess first, ask when needed." Panel 09 then shows the method being tested rather than merely admired. The woman messages, "I'll use rule 2. Okay?" and Kong replies, "State your conclusion and risks." Her thought, "Having a guide helps," matters because she is no longer sending an empty problem upward. The poster "TURN QUESTIONS INTO SKILLS" makes the change visible: judgment is becoming something the team can practice, not something stored only inside Kong.

The warmest punchline arrives when the habit finally starts changing on its own. In panel 10 the glasses-wearing man begins, "Kong, I have a question... wait," then stops himself and says, "I'll try the authority guide first." Kong, relaxed at his desk, thinks, "Congratulations. You can press your own buttons now." Soon after, panel 11 places him beside a RESTROOM sign, staring at his phone in surprise: "Didn't even call me?" Behind him, the woman reports, "Handled. Client confirmed," and the man adds, "Done!" By panel 12 Kong can finally walk away thinking, "Finally, no need to stay online in the restroom." The closing line, "Put down the remote. Let the team come online.", fits the supplied Chapter 34 excerpt as a contemporary echo: work can move through someone without requiring that person to remain the permanent master of every decision.
help-without-becoming-indispensable.quote: All things return to it, yet it does not act as their master; it may be called great.
help-without-becoming-indispensable.practice: Choose one small question that repeatedly comes back to you. Write down the criteria for deciding it, what others may handle without approval, and the point where uncertainty really should be escalated. Let someone try the guide once, then improve the guide from what happens instead of immediately taking the decision back.
help-without-becoming-indispensable.comicTitle: I Became the Office's Only Remote Control
help-without-becoming-indispensable.comicAlt: A twelve-panel Constructivist office comic in bold red, black, and cream. Kong, a dark-haired man in a red jacket, is constantly asked for decisions by a gray-blazer woman and a glasses-wearing man, even while eating noodles and during a half-day away. After his phone fills with urgent team messages, he creates a decision guide covering criteria, authority, and when to ask. His coworkers begin using it, one catches himself before asking Kong another question, and a repeat client issue is solved independently. The story ends with Kong walking toward the restroom, relieved that he no longer has to stay online there, while the team keeps working behind him.

a-relationship-without-new-events.title: No News Today. Can We Still Meet?
a-relationship-without-new-events.teaser: Qing prepares a briefing for coffee with an old friend. Qiu only asked for Qing. A river, shared cake, and a survivable silence gently retire the agenda.
paragraphs: The opening joke is visible right away: Qing sits at the sunlit café table with her laptop, notebook and pen, worrying that she has "nothing new to talk about." Instead of leaving the meeting alone, she turns it into preparation work. In the next panel she writes a full TOPICS list—last week's exhibition, a new café, riverside flowers, a friend's story and a recent film—while telling herself to "prepare a briefing" and "avoid dead air." Qiu's message creates the contrast: "Long time! Coffee Saturday afternoon? No prep. Just a chat." One friend is building a miniature presentation; the other is simply inviting her to show up.

At the riverside café, the plan initially seems to work. Qing cheerfully announces, "I did my homework. Lots to talk about!" while Qiu, resting her face in her hands across the table, replies that she "just wanted to see" her. Qing then starts exactly where her list told her to start: "First, last week's exhibition. Really interesting..." Qiu listens and asks, "Mm-hmm! And then?" The visual rhythm makes that innocent question funny, because the next panel immediately announces "TEN SECONDS OF QUIET" and Qing is already holding her phone, searching for "more material" from the trending list.

The real turning point comes without a lecture. Qiu notices the phone, asks, "Already checking your phone?" and then gently touches Qing's arm while saying, "I invited you, not the trending list." Qing's small "Oh..." is enough. The comic does not turn Qiu into a scolding friend or Qing into a problem to be fixed; the gesture stays affectionate. In the following panel, when Qing asks, "Then... what do we talk about?" Qiu simply answers, "Look at the light on the water for a bit." The story physically moves away from the table and its prepared material toward the riverside itself.

By the railing, the silence starts producing its own kind of conversation. Qing begins, "I was going to say... never mind..." and is allowed to leave the sentence unfinished. Qiu looks at the bright reflections and jokes that the shimmer resembles "coffee spilled across the river." Later, both women laugh while sharing cake, and Qing admits, "I even made an agenda for us." Qiu's reply—"Lucky it wasn't a slide deck"—lands because the comic has already shown how seriously Qing prepared. The humor stays warm: the agenda is gently teased, then replaced by food, observation and company rather than by another supposedly better technique.

The final two panels make the change concrete rather than dramatic. Sitting together again, Qing admits that during the quiet moment she nearly reached for her phone, and Qiu answers, "But you stayed. Nicely done." At sunset, with both women facing each other beside the glowing river, Qing says, "Not much content today." Qiu replies, "Plenty of you, though." The closing line—"The trending list didn't show up. An old friend did."—collects the whole visual journey into one image: the laptop, checklist and phone have faded from importance, while the two friends, the river light, floral cups, daisies and shared cake remain. This connects loosely with the supplied passage's image of "blandness": not as a rule for friendship, but as a contemporary reflection on how something quiet and apparently uneventful can still feel complete.
a-relationship-without-new-events.quote: Thus, when the Way is expressed in words, it is said: bland, ah, without flavor.
a-relationship-without-new-events.practice: Next time you meet someone familiar, try leaving one "must-discuss" topic unprepared. If a few quiet seconds appear, you might wait before reaching for your phone. Look outside, take a sip, or mention one small thing actually in front of you, and see what the conversation does next.
a-relationship-without-new-events.comicTitle: No News Today. Can We Still Meet?
a-relationship-without-new-events.comicAlt: A twelve-panel Impressionist comic in textured blue and yellow brushwork follows Qing, a dark-curly-haired woman in a blue shirt, and Qiu, a brown-haired woman in a cream outfit, meeting at a sunny riverside café. Qing prepares a written list of conversation topics beside a laptop, while Qiu messages that no preparation is needed. Over floral mugs, daisies and cake, Qing begins working through her agenda, then reaches for her phone after ten seconds of silence. Qiu gently touches her arm and says she invited Qing, not the trending list. The friends leave the café, watch sunlight shimmer on the river, joke that it looks like spilled coffee, laugh over cake and tease Qing's meeting agenda. In the final sunset panel, Qing says there was not much content today, and Qiu answers, "Plenty of you, though."

yield-on-the-method.title: I Took the Long Way to Go Straight
yield-on-the-method.teaser: Zhi tries to force a table straight through a narrow doorway. A tape measure, removable legs and a different angle finally get the furniture—and his thinking—unstuck.
paragraphs: The opening joke is built into the geometry. Zhi, in his red shirt, grips an oversized white rectangular table and declares that it will go straight into the room with the tabletop facing the door and "No changing direction!" The black doorway, table legs, and red-blue-yellow blocks make everything look rigidly square, while the woman in blue overalls calmly asks whether they should measure first. Zhi instead pushes harder, turning a simple furniture problem into a contest between one stubbornly straight line and one obviously narrow opening.

Panels 03 through 06 make the failed strategy increasingly physical without anyone being hurt. Zhi leans his whole body into the table, insists that "It has to fit," and then tries "One more push" even after the tabletop is visibly wedged at the doorway. His companion warns that it will get stuck and tells him to stop before scratching it. The turning point arrives when the argument about force finally gives way to the yellow tape measure in Zhi's hands. The joke is that the heroic breakthrough is not more strength at all; it is checking the dimensions.

The lower page turns that change of mind into practical teamwork. Zhi crouches beside the black table frame and notices that the legs are bolted on, while his companion kneels beside him and reinforces the new rhythm: "Check first, then act." In the next panel he removes the fasteners one at a time with a hand tool, loose screws visible on the floor, while she holds a detached black leg. The furniture itself has not become smaller by magic; they have simply looked closely enough to discover which parts can safely change.

Once the legs are off, the same tabletop that failed head-on is tilted diagonally. Zhi carries it at an angle while the woman spots the available space and says, "Sideways gives us room." At the doorway he slows down, turns, and watches the corner instead of charging forward. Afterward he reattaches the table, announcing "Last screw. Done!" while his companion celebrates that there are no broken parts and the destination is unchanged. A couple of loose screws remain visible on the floor; the drawing does not explain whether they are spare fasteners.

The final panel completes the change in mood as well as the furniture move. The table is safely assembled inside the room, Zhi is relaxed in a chair, his companion sits opposite with a cup, and a green potted plant now rests on the tabletop. Their closing lines distinguish the goal from the method: "Same goal. A bend in the method" and "A different angle can make the way easier." Read alongside Chapter 36, this offers a limited contemporary echo of "the soft and weak overcome the strong": flexibility here does not mean abandoning the destination, but using measurement, disassembly, angling, patience, and cooperation instead of treating brute force as proof of commitment.
yield-on-the-method.quote: The soft and weak overcome the strong.
yield-on-the-method.practice: When a small task refuses to move despite repeated effort, try Zhi's later approach: pause, measure the constraint, inspect what can safely change, and ask whether the goal truly requires the method you started with. You may be able to keep the destination while changing the angle.
yield-on-the-method.comicTitle: I Took the Long Way to Go Straight
yield-on-the-method.comicAlt: A two-page, twelve-panel De Stijl-style comic in red, blue, yellow, black, and white. Zhi, a spiky-haired man in a red shirt, first tries to force a large white table straight through a narrow doorway while a bob-haired woman in blue overalls suggests measuring. The table gets stuck, so Zhi uses a yellow tape measure, examines the bolted frame, removes the legs with a hand tool, and carries the tabletop diagonally through the doorway while his companion guides him. He then reassembles the table inside. In the final panel they sit relaxed on opposite sides of the completed table with a green plant and a cup, reflecting that the goal stayed the same even though the method had to bend.

give-a-new-routine-time.title: Two Days into a Habit. Five Systems Already.
give-a-new-routine-time.teaser: Three hours building a tidying system. Three minutes tidying. A one-week experiment gives one small patch of desk a chance before the next app arrives.
paragraphs: The opening joke is visible before the desk has changed much. The woman in the mustard sweater raises a determined fist beside her smiling mug, laptop, books, and a checklist headed "TODAY," where "CLEAR DESK" sits alongside planning tasks, building a new habit, and becoming a "BETTER ME." A wall note says "SMALL CHANGES COUNT," yet the next panel already has her studying "EFFICIENT LIFE PRO" on a screen. The contrast is affectionate: a modest cleaning task has immediately acquired the equipment and ambition of a full productivity project.

The system then becomes more elaborate than the thing it was meant to support. In panel 03 she cheerfully holds three sheets labeled "VERSION 3 TASKS," "VERSION 4 HABITS," and "VERSION 5 LIFE CATEGORIES," while papers, pens, notebooks, and crumpled scraps spread across the desk. Panel 04 turns that escalation into the clearest visual punchline: she grips her head in front of the increasingly cluttered workspace while a sign reads "IDEAL: ORDER / REALITY: ???" Her problem is not a lack of effort; the effort has simply migrated from moving objects to redesigning the method.

Her friend in the teal hoodie creates the turning point by asking a plain question: "How long have you been tidying?" She answers, "All morning? I'm taking it seriously!" The next panel replaces that feeling of busyness with a concrete chart. The laptop shows a tiny slice labeled "TIDYING 3 MIN" beside the dominant "SYSTEM DECORATING 3 HOURS," and her startled "What?" lands the joke without humiliating her. The friend is not presented as the clever winner; he simply gives the pair a clearer picture of where the morning actually went.

The lower page changes the scale of the experiment instead of introducing another grand solution. She writes a "WEEK TRIAL" that assigns one small area to each day—left corner, pens, keyboard, right corner, files, any patch, then review—and the nearby note says "SMALL STEP." In the next panel she wipes one visible patch of tabletop and says, "Just this patch. The rest can wait," while another note answers, "A SMALL AREA COUNTS." She then records the actual sticking points in a notebook: where files should go, too many photos, and papers that are hard to discard. The visible shift is from designing an ideal system to observing specific friction.

The ending tests whether that smaller rhythm can survive temptation. Her friend advises, "Record the problems. Solve them one by one. Don't rush to a new system," and she replies, "Use it first. Improve it as I go." Almost immediately, a phone offers "ALL-IN-ONE ORGANIZER PRO+" with promises of being "SMARTER," "EFFICIENT," and "ONE-TAP." She is visibly tempted, but the last panel shows the phone placed face-down beside the smiling mug as she says, "No. Let the old system survive the weekend first." The sticky note—"HABITS DON'T NEED PERFECTION. LET THEM LIVE, THEN IMPROVE."—and the closing line about organizing one's pace make a contemporary connection with the supplied passage: instead of repeatedly naming, packaging, and remaking everything, the comic imagines what it might look like to hold to a simple practice long enough for change to develop through use. That is a modern reflection, not a claim that the ancient text has only this meaning.
give-a-new-routine-time.quote: The Way is forever nameless. If lords and kings could hold to it, the myriad things would transform of themselves.
give-a-new-routine-time.practice: If you are starting a new habit, give your current method a short fixed trial before replacing it. Do one very small piece today and write down the specific thing that actually slows you down. After several real obstacles have appeared, decide whether the tool needs changing—or whether the existing method simply needs another day of use.
give-a-new-routine-time.comicTitle: Two Days into a Habit. Five Systems Already.
give-a-new-routine-time.comicAlt: A twelve-panel handmade-clay-style comic set at a warm, cluttered desk. A brown-haired woman in a mustard sweater begins a desk-tidying habit, tries a productivity app, creates several spreadsheet versions, and ends up with a messier workspace. Her brown-haired friend in a teal hoodie shows a chart revealing three minutes of tidying versus three hours of system decorating. She then tries a one-week plan with one small desk area per day, wipes a single patch, lists concrete sticking points, and agrees to solve them one at a time. When a new all-in-one organizing app appears on her phone, she resists it, places the phone down, and decides to let the old system survive the weekend first.

substance-before-a-good-image.title: Most of My Hard Work Is Proving I Work Hard
substance-before-a-good-image.teaser: Alex posts five-minute updates about working, then has nothing useful to report. One working module finally gives his next update something to say.
paragraphs: The opening joke is not that Alex is avoiding work. He looks almost excessively prepared for it. In his navy suit, he photographs a desk stacked with books labeled PROJECT, RESEARCH, DESIGN, and PROGRESS, while a board announces PLAN, FOCUS, EXECUTE, and FINISH. Even his mug says "GOOD WORK BETTER ME." The scene has every visual signal of serious productivity, yet the phone is already becoming the main character: the carefully arranged evidence of working is taking up space that could have gone to the work itself.

That joke grows through the next updates. Alex photographs the setup again after five minutes, then his feed neatly records "STARTING!," "ORGANIZING!," and "THINKING!" at 09:05, 09:10, and 09:15. When his coworker asks how the project is going, he answers by holding up the phone and pointing to his constant progress. The turning point comes at report time. The board beside him still has RESULTS, DATA, and NEXT STEPS unchecked, and in the next panel his coworker asks the painfully practical question: is there anything they can actually put in the report? Alex looks down at the phone and admits there probably is not yet.

The lower page changes the behavior without turning Alex into a miraculous productivity machine. He switches off FIVE-MINUTE UPDATES, DAILY FRAGMENTS, and RANDOM PHOTOS, while leaving ESSENTIAL SYNC on and keeping MILESTONES and IMPORTANT ISSUES checked. The black mug beside him now reads "LESS BROADCAST MORE WORK," turning the earlier mug joke into a quieter reminder. With fewer status rituals competing for attention, he works on Module A. The visible checklist covers DATA, IMPLEMENTATION, INITIAL TESTS, and OUTPUT, while the progress bar remains at 80%, making it clear that this is meaningful progress rather than a claim that the whole project is finished.

The comic also keeps the process imperfect. Alex tells his coworker that he has a working first version and will organize the data before syncing with her. Later he admits that he hit a snag midway and spent time solving it. The important change is not silence: he still communicates, and she still offers help and review. What disappears is the need to broadcast every intermediate motion as proof of effort. Their conversation is now attached to something concrete—a working version, a solved problem, and a reviewable result—rather than a stream of photos showing that activity is happening.

The ending makes the contrast visible on the laptop. Instead of a gallery of status updates, the project stage report is one page, led by "Core first version completed," with GOAL ACHIEVED, CORE FUNCTION DEMO, DATA RESULTS, and NEXT STEPS, plus attachments such as DATA DETAILS.xlsx and TEST RECORDS.pdf. In the final panel Alex leans back beneath a note reading "LESS BROADCAST MORE WORK," while the page closes with "Looking busy fades. What you make is what stays." Read beside Chapter 38, this can be a contemporary reflection on preferring substance to display: not an instruction to stop communicating, but an invitation to let communication gather around work that has actually become usable.
substance-before-a-good-image.quote: Therefore the great person dwells in what is substantial, not in what is thin; dwells in what is real, not in what is showy.
substance-before-a-good-image.practice: Choose one thing you are already working on and skip one unnecessary progress display today. Use that small pocket of time to finish a piece someone can actually open, read, test, or use. When you do need to sync, share that concrete result instead of documenting every step that led to it.
substance-before-a-good-image.comicTitle: Most of My Hard Work Is Proving I Work Hard
substance-before-a-good-image.comicAlt: A twelve-panel blue-gray office comic follows Alex, a dark-haired man in a navy suit, from constant productivity posting to more focused work. He photographs his desk, laptop, books, and progress repeatedly, then discovers that his report has no results, data, or next steps to show. He turns off unnecessary update broadcasts, keeps essential syncs, develops Module A to a visible 80% with a working first version, solves a problem, reviews progress with a bob-haired coworker in a white blouse, and finishes with a concise project report and attachments. The final office scene shows Alex leaning back beside a note reading "LESS BROADCAST MORE WORK."

the-work-beneath-a-result.title: The Latte Gets Likes. The Foundations Don’t.
the-work-beneath-a-result.teaser: The new latte is ready for its close-up. The cups, milk and floor are not. A cafe discovers that a photogenic drink still needs unphotogenic foundations.
paragraphs: The opening joke is wonderfully concrete: the woman in the green apron bends over a carefully poured latte with her phone held like a second piece of café equipment. The chalkboard announces the new Mountain Latte, and she declares, "Gorgeous! This latte art needs a post!" In the next panel she is still searching for better light and predicting that the drink will go viral. The composition makes the contrast visible before anyone explains it: the latte is polished and camera-ready, while the everyday machinery of the café is already beginning to strain around it.

That strain becomes explicit when the bearded man in the brown apron appears beside stacks of cups and warns, "Running low on cups and milk. Restock now?" She answers, "Wait! A few more photos. I’ll post first!" The humor is gentle because nobody is behaving like a villain; they are simply looking at different layers of the same job. One person is focused on the exciting new product, while the other is noticing the supplies that allow any product to reach a customer at all.

The turning point arrives through props rather than philosophy. Customers ask whether the new latte is still available and why the wait is taking so long; the woman realizes they are out of cups and tries to improvise with other mugs. Then a cup and liquid are visibly spilled across the floor, a bright yellow "CAUTION WET FLOOR" sign appears, and she warns that the floor is slippery. By panel 06, the bearded coworker is mopping while offering to clean and restock, and she admits that being absorbed in the photos made her miss what was happening around her. The polished launch has literally met the floor.

The lower page turns that embarrassment into cooperation. In panel 07 he washes and restocks cups while she agrees to sort order priorities. In panel 08 they make the invisible work visible on a large TODAY board: cups, stock, cleaning, orders and drinks, and photos when quiet. Panel 09 shows labeled containers for beans, milk, and syrup while the rush-hour menu is simplified. By panel 10 she can pour another latte and joke, "Enough cups. Clean counter. Nobody panicking!" The chalkboard reading "THREE DRINKS IN PROGRESS" is funny precisely because ordinary stability has become an achievement worth announcing.

The ending quietly reverses the opening idea of what deserves attention. Only after the workflow settles does the woman return to photographing the latte, now saying that it looks good and tastes consistent and is therefore worth sharing; behind her, the board says "NEW DRINKS THIS AFTERNOON." In the final panel, the glamorous latte disappears and everyone raises plain white mugs instead. Her line, "Today’s star: a day with no disasters!" turns the earlier hunger for visibility into a joke about dependable basics. The supplied Daodejing line can be read alongside this as one contemporary association: what is elevated depends on what is lower and less celebrated. The comic does not present that as the only meaning of the passage; it simply lets a café make the relationship visible.
the-work-beneath-a-result.quote: Therefore, what is noble must take what is humble as its root, and what is high must take what is low as its foundation.
the-work-beneath-a-result.practice: Choose one thing you are eager to make impressive and look underneath it for one unglamorous supporting step: restocking, checking, cleaning, confirming, simplifying, or leaving enough time. Try strengthening that layer first, without rushing to display the result, and notice whether the visible work becomes easier to sustain.
the-work-beneath-a-result.comicTitle: The Latte Gets Likes. The Foundations Don’t.
the-work-beneath-a-result.comicAlt: A twelve-panel Post-Impressionist café comic in muted blue, green, and ochre tones. A woman with a dark bun, white blouse, and green apron repeatedly photographs a mountain-pattern latte while a bearded man in a brown apron notices cups and milk running low. Waiting customers, empty cups, a spilled drink, and a yellow CAUTION WET FLOOR sign turn the photo session into a small café crisis. The man mops, washes cups, and restocks while the pair reorganize their work on a TODAY board listing cups, stock, cleaning, orders and drinks, and photos when quiet. Labeled containers for beans, milk, and syrup appear as the workflow settles. Later the woman pours calmly beneath a THREE DRINKS IN PROGRESS board, photographs the latte only when the café is quiet, and finally joins the man and other customers or coworkers in raising plain white mugs. The closing text reads, "Good work often starts where nobody is looking," followed by "Daodejing - Chapter 39 - A contemporary reflection."

return-to-what-worked.title: My Smart Home Went on Strike. I Found a Switch.
return-to-what-worked.teaser: The internet fails. Xin tells the dark room to turn on the lights ten times. An old lamp and a manual switch finally join this very futuristic conversation.
paragraphs: The opening makes Xin's confidence almost as visible as the technology itself. In the blue-and-gold space-age apartment, he stands beside a sleek control panel labeled LIGHTS, CURTAINS, FAN and ALL CONNECTED, while the futuristic city glows outside. He announces that everything is linked, and the woman answers, "Just say the word? Brilliant!" In the next panel he is already reclining with a mug, pleased that he can "Run the house without getting up." The relaxed pose, polished interface and optimistic "The future!" make the later failure funnier because the comic first lets the convenience look completely convincing.

The joke turns sharply when the apartment goes dark. A large screen reports CONNECTION FAILED and CHECK NETWORK while Xin stares at his phone in alarm. The next panel makes the problem physical and ridiculous: he stands alone in the darkness with his hands around his mouth, repeatedly shouting "Lights on!" into the room. The caption confirms that he does this ten times, but nothing changes. By panel 05 he has collapsed onto the floor and admits, "I've been giving the air a speech." The woman, laughing beside him, replies, "Impressive delivery, though!" The humor comes from effort increasing while the result remains exactly zero.

The turning point is deliberately small. Instead of arguing about whether smart homes are good or bad, the woman brings out a glowing old lamp and a manual switch and says, "Old lamp tonight. Add a manual switch. Get the room usable, then troubleshoot." Xin initially calls the switch backward, but immediately adds that light matters more right now. On the lower page, the warm lamp is already working, and Xin installs the manual switch while the woman watches. His line, "No internet needed. Press it: light," is almost comically plain after the earlier futuristic promises, yet that plainness is precisely what changes the situation.

Once the room is usable again, the comic returns to technology rather than rejecting it. Xin opens a laptop to check the router and smart hub, while a neat stack of books is labeled SMART HOME, NETWORK SETTINGS, TROUBLESHOOTING and BACKUP PLAN. The woman says they can keep the technology, "Just not all our eggs in one basket." The system is eventually restored, and the lights, curtains and fan respond again. In the next relaxed scene, Xin leans back on the sofa while the woman holds a cat, visually showing that the crisis has passed. Convenience has returned, but it now sits beside a backup rather than replacing one.

The final two panels make that change visible. Xin points to a wall display that keeps the manual switch and smart controls side by side: MANUAL / WORKS OFFLINE, SMART / CONVENIENT ONLINE, followed by LIGHTS, CURTAINS and FAN and the line TWO WAYS. LESS WORRY. He says, "Keep the switch. Keep the smart system. Two ways to get light," and the woman answers, "Now that's smart living!" In the closing panel they sit with the cat and look over the glowing futuristic city while the old lamp shines beside them. Xin says that returning to a switch is not the end of progress but a move closer to what they need. Read alongside "Reversal is the movement of the Way," this can be taken as one modest everyday connection: moving forward may sometimes include returning to a neglected basic function. The comic does not present that as the only meaning of the line; it simply uses one failed network and one reachable switch to make the idea concrete.
return-to-what-worked.quote: Reversal is the movement of the Way.
return-to-what-worked.practice: Choose one convenience you rely on and imagine it unavailable for an evening. Is there a simple backup that would keep the essential function working? You might add one practical alternative, then keep enjoying the smarter system without turning old and new methods into a contest.
return-to-what-worked.comicTitle: My Smart Home Went on Strike. I Found a Switch.
return-to-what-worked.comicAlt: A twelve-panel retro-futurist comic shows Xin, a tousled dark-haired man in a grey jumpsuit, proudly demonstrating a fully connected smart apartment to a short-haired woman in an orange planet shirt. When the internet fails, he repeatedly shouts "Lights on!" into a dark room and jokes that he has been giving the air a speech. The woman brings an old bronze lamp and a manual wall switch, restoring light before they troubleshoot the router and smart hub. After the smart system returns, they keep both manual and connected controls. The final scene shows the pair and a cat facing a glowing futuristic city while the lamp shines beside them.

slower-while-learning.title: I Started Learning. Now I Can't Draw.
slower-while-learning.teaser: Learning perspective makes a happy sketcher feel he cannot draw. An old floating table leg and one very tired-looking cup reveal what has really changed: he can finally see the problems.
paragraphs: The opening makes the contradiction of learning more and feeling less capable immediately visible. In panel 01, the young man in a white T-shirt and round glasses smiles over a lively street sketch while a cat sits nearby, the mug declares "DRAWING IS FUN!", and handwritten praise such as "GENIUS!" and "NOT BAD!" surrounds him. One panel later, the mood flips: perspective books, rulers, construction lines, crumpled paper, and a crowded desk replace that easy confidence. He grips his hair and says that after learning perspective, "every line picked a fight." The joke works because nothing dramatic has happened except that he has learned enough to notice how unruly those lines really are.

Panel 03 pushes the frustration into visual comedy. The young man collapses across a table buried under perspective diagrams, discarded sheets, pencils, erasers, and books labeled "PERSPECTIVE," "STRUCTURE," "LIGHT & SHADOW," and "FIGURE...." His description of the practice sheets as "more like a crash site" is almost literal in the composition. The turning point arrives when the woman in the dark top produces one of his older drawings. Instead of telling him he has suddenly become worse, she points to a table leg that appears to float. His surprised "Huh?" becomes important: the flaw was already there, but now he has the eyes to recognize it.

The woman does not repair the old drawing for him or add another complicated lesson. She reduces the task to the real cup sitting on the table: "Skip the whole room today. One cup." In panel 07, his first attempt makes the rim look like a flattened pancake, and his thought bubble jokes that the cup seems exhausted after finishing work. In panel 08, she physically rotates a mug and asks him to notice how the rim remains an ellipse while its visible thickness changes with the angle. She explicitly refuses to draw it for him. The action shifts the lesson from collecting more instructions to looking more carefully at the object already in front of him.

The next panels show improvement as a messy process rather than a magical correction. He studies the curve, adjusts the handle connection, erases repeatedly, and ends up surrounded by so many crumbs and crumpled scraps that he jokes he has produced more eraser debris than art. Panel 10 places the "FIRST TRY" beside the "THIRD TRY," making the changes concrete: the later cup has a rounder rim, clearer perspective, a more convincing handle connection, and a shadow. His comment that finding what is wrong matters more than speed shows a new kind of progress. He is no longer measuring success only by whether a drawing looks finished quickly.

The ending keeps the result deliberately imperfect. When the woman asks what he noticed, he jokes that he used to draw so fast that his mistakes could not catch him; now, by slowing down, he can see more details. In the final panel he beams while holding up the cup sketch and says, "Not perfect. But now I know what each line is doing. That feels good!" The closing caption, "Seeing the problem is part of learning," connects naturally with the chapter's Daoist excerpt without claiming the comic is a literal interpretation. One possible contemporary reflection is that progress can temporarily feel like retreat when greater understanding makes previously invisible problems visible.
slower-while-learning.quote: Therefore an established saying goes: The bright Way seems dim; advancing on the Way seems like retreating; the level Way seems rough.
slower-while-learning.practice: If something recently feels harder the more you learn about it, try shrinking the task to the size of one cup. Observe one specific problem, change one thing, and compare before and after. The aim is not to force a perfect result, but to see whether you can describe more clearly what changed and why.
slower-while-learning.comicTitle: I Started Learning. Now I Can't Draw.
slower-while-learning.comicAlt: Two-page black-and-white manga set in a drawing studio. A tousle-haired young man with round glasses first enjoys sketching freely, then becomes overwhelmed by perspective books, rulers, construction lines, and piles of failed practice sheets. A woman in a dark top shows him an old drawing with a floating table leg, then asks him to practice only one real cup. He draws a squashed rim, jokes that the cup looks exhausted, watches her rotate the mug to demonstrate changing perspective, and repeatedly erases and redraws it. His first and third attempts are compared side by side, showing a rounder rim, improved handle connection, clearer perspective, and a shadow. In the final panel he smiles broadly while holding the still-imperfect cup drawing and says that now he knows what each line is doing.

show-one-useful-step.title: A Hundred Explanations. Or One Cup Together.
show-one-useful-step.teaser: Temperature, pressure, grind, timing: the coffee lesson is becoming an academic conference. Then they try making one cup together, nearly giving the coffee a free-fall experiment along the way.
paragraphs: The opening joke is that the more carefully the man explains, the harder coffee seems to make. Standing beside the silver espresso machine, he points through a whole technical vocabulary: grind, distribute, tamp, extract, about 92 degrees Celsius, and nine bars. The woman in the brown sweater rests her head on one hand and admits, "So many terms. I can't remember them all." Behind them, botanical coffee drawings and the little "Anatomy of Coffee" display make the room look increasingly like a classroom, while the empty cup quietly reminds us that nobody has actually made coffee yet.

The explanation keeps expanding. A wall diagram compares "TOO COARSE," "ABOUT RIGHT," and "TOO FINE," then the man demonstrates tamping with "15–20 kilos of force" and describes a shot lasting "25–30 seconds" for 36 grams. Each answer produces another anxious question: "Will I break it?" and "Will I press the wrong button?" By panel 05, even the visual language has become heavy: a stack of books labeled Grind, Distribute, Tamp, Attach Handle, Extract, and Temperature / Pressure / Time sits beside them. The turning point arrives when the man finally notices the obvious problem and says, "Talking alone is a lot. What if we try this?"

The second page changes the teaching method rather than adding another explanation. The man says, "I'll do one. Watch along," and the long lecture collapses into a simple visual sequence: GRIND, TAMP, EXTRACT. Then panel 08 makes the new rule explicit: "Remember the actions first, not the vocabulary." Four close-up boxes show GRIND, LEVEL, TAMP, and LOCK IN. The woman answers, "I can follow this!" The important shift is visible in their bodies as well as their words: instead of sitting beside a growing pile of information, they are now leaning over the machine and doing something together.

Once the woman takes over, mistakes become small, local, and fixable. In panel 09 she presses the tamper herself, with loose coffee grounds scattered across the counter, and asks, "Like this?" The man does not restart the entire lesson; he simply points to the bed and says, "A little more level here. That's it." In the next panel he points out where the cup should go, and she jokes, "Oh! Nearly gave the coffee a free-fall experiment!" That warm joke matters because the error is not turned into evidence that she cannot do it. It is just the next thing to adjust.

The payoff is deliberately ordinary. In panel 11, espresso finally streams from the machine into the large white cup, and the woman leans in with delighted surprise: "It's coming out! Actual coffee!" The man answers, "No academic conference required." By the final panel, both have moved away from the machinery and are holding cups at the table. He says that knowledge has moved "from my mouth to my hands," and she finishes the thought with "And into our cups!" The closing line, "Fewer explanations. One cup made together," offers a contemporary echo of Chapter 43: not a literal translation of the ancient text, but a small domestic example of how less verbal control and more shared action can sometimes make understanding possible.
show-one-useful-step.quote: Teaching without words, the benefit of non-action—few under heaven can attain this.
show-one-useful-step.practice: If you notice yourself repeating the same explanation today, try turning one part of it into a shared demonstration. Do it once together, then let the other person take the next step. Add a short correction only when a real difficulty appears, and see whether the task becomes clearer through action.
show-one-useful-step.comicTitle: A Hundred Explanations. Or One Cup Together.
show-one-useful-step.comicAlt: Two-page, twelve-panel illustrated comic in a warm cream-and-blue botanical café setting. A glasses-wearing man in a blue shirt first overwhelms a bun-haired woman in a brown sweater with espresso terminology, grind diagrams, tamping force, timing, and stacked instruction books. He then switches to demonstrating the actions on a silver espresso machine. She grinds, levels, tamps, spills some grounds, nearly forgets the cup, successfully pulls a shot, and finally sits with him drinking coffee. The ending reads: "Fewer explanations. One cup made together."

what-a-new-opportunity-costs.title: A Pay Rise. Three Time Zones Included.
what-a-new-opportunity-costs.teaser: A 50% raise sparkles in gold. Then three time zones arrive with it. Before accepting, she puts the offer on a calendar and negotiates the parts that can change.
paragraphs: The opening turns the pleasure of a raise into something almost physically oversized. The woman in the emerald suit holds a JOB OFFER marked ANNUAL SALARY +50%, while an enormous golden +50% soon fills the next panel behind her. Her imagined rewards float around it: a city apartment, travel, a handbag, a restaurant meal and a brighter future. The Art Deco rays, dark green interiors and gold geometry make the opportunity look like a stage premiere. That exaggeration is also the first joke: the salary has already become enormous before the rest of her life has had time to enter the picture.

The cream-suited man does not puncture her excitement; he simply asks, "What are the conditions?" The visual answer arrives as three compact slices of ordinary life. Her commute stretches from one hour to two, overseas work produces frequent night meetings, and family time becomes harder to protect. Three clocks above the nighttime desk turn the title's "three time zones" into a literal prop, while the conversation with her mother gives the cost a human scale. The woman is not suddenly told the opportunity is bad. She is simply shown that the extra money is not the only thing being exchanged.

The turning point is practical rather than dramatic. In panel 07, the woman sits with a notebook and a board divided into BENEFITS and COSTS, listing higher pay, a bigger platform, challenge and growth beside commute x2, night calls, less family time, energy and schedule changes. Then she and the man rehearse the conversation instead of rehearsing a refusal. Her request sheet names remote days, a travel allowance, limits on night calls, family time and team working arrangements. The line "No automatic refusal, no automatic yes" captures what the pictures are doing: replacing a vague reaction with negotiable terms and visible boundaries.

The video-call panel makes the trade-off specific. The recruiter on the screen confirms two remote days each week and a commuting allowance, while two weekly night meetings remain fixed for the overseas team. The checklist visibly marks the first two items while leaving the night-meeting condition separate. The next panel then places those abstract terms into a real week: Tuesday and Thursday carry 20:00-22:00 Night Call blocks, Wednesday reserves 18:30-20:00 for Family Dinner, Friday gets coffee, and the weekend becomes two simple trees marked Rest. The joke is gentle but useful: an offer can sound manageable in a sentence and look very different once it occupies colored squares on a calendar.

By panel 11, the woman has decided to accept. She does not call the offer perfect; she says it is "Worth choosing at this stage," while the man answers, "A decision that fits you." The final panel softens the office calculation with coffee, cake, flowers and both characters smiling. Her closing thought, "Salary is addition. Life needs the whole balance sheet," is followed by the man's reminder that living well matters in the long run, while the footer lands on "A salary can sparkle. A calendar tells the truth." As a contemporary reflection, this can sit beside Chapter 44's attention to contentment and knowing when to stop: not as the only meaning of the classical passage, but as one everyday way of noticing what is enough, what has a cost, and what one is genuinely willing to carry.
what-a-new-opportunity-costs.quote: Therefore, knowing contentment avoids disgrace; knowing when to stop avoids danger; thus one can endure.
what-a-new-opportunity-costs.practice: When an opportunity looks especially attractive, try making your own BENEFITS and COSTS page, then place the important conditions into an actual week. Mark what could be negotiated, what would remain fixed and what time you want to protect. The exercise is not meant to produce an automatic yes or no; it simply lets the full shape of the choice become visible.
what-a-new-opportunity-costs.comicTitle: A Pay Rise. Three Time Zones Included.
what-a-new-opportunity-costs.comicAlt: Two-page, twelve-panel Art Deco comic in dark green and gold. A short black-haired woman in an emerald suit receives a job offer with a 50% salary increase and imagines a bigger apartment, travel and restaurants. A dark-haired man in a cream suit asks about the conditions, leading to scenes of a doubled commute, overseas night meetings, three clocks and reduced family time. The woman lists benefits and costs, rehearses negotiation requests, speaks with a recruiter by video, wins two remote days and a commuting allowance, accepts two fixed weekly night calls, maps the arrangement onto a weekly calendar, and ultimately accepts the offer. The final scene shows the woman and man smiling over coffee and cake beneath the closing line, "A salary can sparkle. A calendar tells the truth."

useful-before-perfect.title: My Project Retired Before It Launched
useful-before-perfect.teaser: Version 38. One rounded corner still needs a philosophical summit. A missing contact button finally redirects the project toward three real testers and its first useful feedback.
paragraphs: The opening joke is built from wonderfully specific evidence of endless revision. Beside the man are books labeled Version 35, Version 36, Version 37, and Version 38, while a sticky note announces Version 38 again and his mug says "JUST A LITTLE BETTER." He is already staring at a polished "My Work" page, yet his speech bubble promises "One more tweak." The absurdity peaks in panel 02, where a large brass magnifying glass nearly fills the scene as he studies a blue START button and decides its rounded corner "could be a little rounder." The solemn, oil-painted studio, antique books, sculpture busts, and warm academic atmosphere make this microscopic design crisis feel comically monumental.

The woman does not argue that visual polish is worthless; she tests whether the page can do its job. In panel 03 she asks, "Can I use your portfolio site yet?" and the man answers, "Let me smooth out the details." His definition of "details" becomes the next joke: he presents two nearly identical buttons as options A and B, complete with competing personalities—"CLEAN / MODERN / RESTRAINED" versus "SOFT / FRIENDLY / WARM." Her dry reply, "...It’s one corner," punctures the presentation without turning it into a fight. The comic keeps the disagreement practical: he is looking at subtle visual distinctions, while she is trying to find out whether another person can actually move through the site.

Panel 05 supplies the turning point with a phone instead of another aesthetic debate. The woman holds up the portfolio page and says, "Nice page. But I can’t even find how to contact you." The phone itself confirms the problem with the visible notice "No contact details." Meanwhile, the man is still bent over his magnifying glass and the nearby mug now declares "PIXELS ARE JUSTICE," extending the visual joke. In panel 06, she changes the question completely: "Let’s stop holding meetings about corners. List the minimum that makes it usable." His surprised "The minimum?" matters because, for the first time, attention moves away from how finished the interface feels and toward what another person must actually be able to do.

The lower page turns that new question into concrete action. The notebook in panel 07 lists four visible checks: "See your work," "Find you," "Leave feedback," and "Open on a phone." The man agrees: "Fine. Usable first." The website then gains clear CONTACT, FEEDBACK, and SEND SUGGESTION areas, and a phone is used to check the mobile version. His old habit has not vanished: in panel 09 the magnifying glass returns and he starts, "Wait. The spacing needs half a breath..." The woman answers, "Let them click first. Discuss its aura later." That line works because the comic lets perfectionism reappear once more, but this time it no longer gets to stop the release.

The ending stays deliberately small. Instead of a grand public launch, panel 10 shows "TEST VERSION RELEASED" and "SHARED WITH 3 TESTERS." Then something new appears in panel 11: an actual user message—"Worked smoothly. Sent you my brief. Feedback was easy to find." The man’s surprised "Someone actually used it!" is answered by the woman: "Look. Your work’s alive." In the final panel, the magnifying glass is lying unused on the desk, the screen shows two new suggestions—"Love the style!" and "Please add filters."—and the stacked books read "MORE TO IMPROVE," "ALREADY MOVING," and "THANK YOU USERS." Read alongside the supplied line from the Daodejing, this offers a limited contemporary connection: something can remain visibly unfinished and still begin to serve a real use. The comic does not celebrate carelessness; it distinguishes between what must work now and what can improve in the next version.
useful-before-perfect.quote: Great completion seems incomplete, yet its use is never exhausted.
useful-before-perfect.practice: If you have something that keeps waiting for one more refinement, try writing four or five minimum-use checks like the notebook in the comic: Can people see it? Can they reach you? Can they complete the main action? Can they leave feedback? Does the key path work on the device they will actually use? Then consider sharing a small test version with two or three real users before deciding what the next revision needs.
useful-before-perfect.comicTitle: My Project Retired Before It Launched
useful-before-perfect.comicAlt: A twelve-panel, warm brown oil-painted comic set in an antique book-filled design studio. A tousled brown-haired man in a cream shirt repeatedly refines a portfolio website, examining a blue button through a large brass magnifying glass and comparing nearly identical rounded corners. A brown-haired woman in a navy jacket tests the site on a phone, points out that it has no contact details, writes a four-item minimum-usability checklist, and encourages a small release. The site gains contact and feedback options, is shared with three testers, receives a successful user message and two suggestions, and ends with the magnifying glass resting on the desk beside books labeled "MORE TO IMPROVE," "ALREADY MOVING," and "THANK YOU USERS."

let-an-upgrade-wait.title: My Phone Was Fine. I Worried on Its Behalf.
let-an-upgrade-wait.teaser: A new phone ad puts an old phone on trial. After a magnifying glass, a storage cleanup and a sunset photo, its owner starts investigating actual needs instead of imagined obsolescence.
paragraphs: The opening joke is that the phone has done almost nothing wrong before it is put on trial. In the neon-purple first panel, the man in the pink hoodie lights up at an ad promising "Better photos" and "Smarter AI," then immediately turns suspicious of the scratched phone already in his hand. A floating checklist escalates the mood with "BLURRY PHOTOS?," "SLOW?," "OUTDATED LOOK?," and "TIME TO REPLACE?" Yet when the woman in purple asks what actually bothers him during use, he admits that photos and navigation still work fine. The visual punch line peaks when he literally raises a magnifying glass to inspect scratches, battery worries, and old-looking edges while a caption declares, "WITH A MAGNIFIER, EVERYTHING IS A PROBLEM."

The woman does not try to win an abstract argument about whether buying a new phone is good or bad. Instead, she keeps bringing the conversation back to observable problems. After teasing him for "using a magnifying glass to hunt for flaws," she points out that the phone still takes photos, navigates, and handles daily use. Panel 06 ends with her asking them to look at "what the actual problem is," and the lower page turns that sentence into action: they sit together at a laptop, back up photos, videos, files, and contacts, and watch the backup indicator reach 78 percent. The comedy shifts from inspecting cosmetic defects to doing very ordinary maintenance.

That maintenance produces the first concrete surprise. In panel 08, the storage display changes from 3GB free to 82GB free after they clear cache, remove duplicates, sort photos, and remove unused apps. The man looks delighted rather than worried, while the woman laughs beside him and says that sometimes the phone is not failing; they are simply asking it to hold too much. The comic does not pretend that storage cleanup magically solves every hardware concern. Instead, it shows why separating one specific problem from the general feeling of "my phone is old" can change the decision from a vague replacement impulse into something testable.

Battery life receives the same practical treatment rather than a command to keep suffering with the old device. Panel 09 shows a "BATTERY SERVICE" interface with fictional illustrative quotes for official, authorized, and reputable third-party options, plus a notebook labeled "EXAMPLE QUOTES" and checked steps such as backup completed, storage cleared, and battery options checked. The man says he will consider a battery replacement first, and the woman notes that it could extend the phone's useful life for less than replacing the whole device. In the next panel they explicitly leave the door open to buying a new phone if a fresh battery still does not meet his needs: "No forced thrift, but no impulse buy either."

The final two panels move attention away from settings screens and back toward the world outside them. At a glowing orange-and-pink sunset, the man raises the same old phone that was previously examined through a magnifying glass and discovers that one quick photo still looks lovely. The woman answers that some beautiful things do not require the newest device. In the last panel both characters are smiling, the man jokes that "The sky updated. The phone can wait," and the closing line says, "Sometimes the world needs no upgrade. We need another look." Read alongside the supplied excerpt, this works as a contemporary reflection on sufficiency rather than a literal translation: the comic does not say that nothing should ever be replaced, only that noticing what is already sufficient can create more room for a deliberate choice.
let-an-upgrade-wait.quote: Therefore, when you know the sufficiency of enough, you will always have enough.
let-an-upgrade-wait.practice: The next time you suddenly want to replace something that still works, try writing down three specific things that are actually bothering you. Pick one that can be checked, cleaned up, repaired, or tested now. If those concrete steps still leave the item unable to meet your needs, replacing it can then be a considered choice rather than a reaction to the feeling of being behind.
let-an-upgrade-wait.comicTitle: My Phone Was Fine. I Worried on Its Behalf.
let-an-upgrade-wait.comicAlt: A two-page, twelve-panel vaporwave comic in purple, pink, and blue neon. A tousle-haired man in a pink hoodie sees a next-generation phone advertisement, worries that his scratched phone is obsolete, and even inspects it with a magnifying glass while a woman in a purple jacket questions what is actually wrong. They back up files on a laptop, clear storage from 3GB free to 82GB free, review fictional battery-service quotes, and agree to reconsider a new phone only if practical fixes still do not meet his needs. At sunset, he photographs the skyline with his old phone and is surprised by the beautiful result. The final panel shows both characters smiling as the comic closes with the idea that sometimes the world needs no upgrade; we need another look.

beginner-again.title: Day-One Beginner. Full-Time Expert Persona.
beginner-again.teaser: A seasoned professional tries managing clay like a team. The clay resigns into a heap. One honest question and several crooked attempts finally make room for a beginner.
paragraphs: The opening joke is that the man brings his workplace confidence straight into a pottery studio. In his fresh brown apron and glasses, he announces, "First pottery class. I'll pick it up fast. I'm a seasoned professional, after all." One panel later, both hands are gripping the spinning clay while he orders it, "Listen to me! Hold steady! Keep up!" The line about being good at managing teams makes the mismatch even funnier: the clay is not an employee, and his commanding posture cannot persuade it to cooperate. By panel 03, the pot has collapsed into a lumpy heap and bits of clay are flying while his expression changes from certainty to alarm.

The first real turn comes through another beginner rather than the teacher. Holding her own small piece, the blue-aproned classmate cheerfully says, "My first time too. Can't center it. Any tips?" That simple question leaves the man scratching his head and answering, "Well... actually, I..." The confident persona suddenly has nowhere to hide. In the next panel, he does something much more useful than pretending: he raises his hand and asks the teacher, "How do I center the clay?" The physical change matters too. Instead of issuing commands over the wheel, he makes room for someone else to stand beside him and show him what to notice.

The teacher does not magically finish the piece for him. She guides his hands toward the spinning clay and says, "Relax your hands. Feel where the clay's weight sits as it turns." On the next page, the lesson becomes even more concrete: "Lighter hands. Let it turn. Feel the center. No rush." He concentrates hard, repeating, "Slowly. Steady hands. Find the center," while the thought bubble reframes the whole situation as "NOT BOSSING IT AROUND. WORKING WITH IT." The comedy continues because understanding the idea does not produce instant mastery. In panel 09 the clay tilts again, fragments scatter, and he admits, "Off-center again! Still rushing."

That second failure becomes the gentler turning point. The teacher responds, "That's okay. Hands on both sides. Gently toward the center. Feel it change," and the man simply answers, "I'll try again." By panel 11, he is holding a visibly imperfect bowl: its rim is uneven, its shape is a little crooked, and nothing about it looks exhibition-ready. Yet his smile is much more relaxed than the proud expression in the opening panel. His line, "A bit crooked. But I actually made it!" makes the achievement specific. The final joke, "Thick resume. Thin bowl base. Today, learn the bowl," does not erase his professional experience; it just stops asking that experience to prove he should already be good at pottery.

Placed beside the line "For learning, one gains daily; for the Way, one loses daily," the comic works as a contemporary reflection rather than a literal translation. Pottery certainly requires gaining technique, coordination, and experience, but this particular lesson also involves letting some things fall away: the urge to look competent immediately, the instinct to control every movement, and the rush to turn a first attempt into evidence of expertise. The closing caption, "Some things go better when we stop rushing to be good at them," keeps the connection modest. The story does not claim that less is always better than more; it shows one beginner making enough space to learn what the clay is actually doing.
beginner-again.quote: For learning, one gains daily; for the Way, one loses daily.
beginner-again.practice: The next time you enter a field where you are genuinely new, try replacing one performance of competence with one concrete question. Ask the equivalent of "How do I center the clay?" Then make one attempt, notice what changes, and let today's task be only today's small piece of learning.
beginner-again.comicAlt: A two-page, twelve-panel low-poly comic in a warm pottery studio. A brown-haired man with glasses and a brown apron starts his first pottery class by confidently treating the spinning clay like a team he can manage, only for the pot to collapse. A fellow beginner exposes his lack of experience with a friendly question, after which he asks a dark-haired teacher in a blue apron for help. She guides his hands, tells him to relax, feel the clay's weight, and move gently toward the center. He fails again, tries once more, and finally holds up a slightly crooked handmade bowl with a broad smile. The story ends with the joke, "Thick resume. Thin bowl base. Today, learn the bowl," and the closing reflection, "Some things go better when we stop rushing to be good at them."

ask-how-they-want-help.title: The Comfort Package Nobody Ordered
ask-how-they-want-help.teaser: He was only sad. Now he has an itinerary. Hiking, dinner and karaoke give way to the comfort he actually ordered: a quiet walk and help with one phone call.
paragraphs: The opening joke comes from the sharp mismatch between their tempos. In the first panel, the man in the blue jacket is slumped beside two patterned mugs and says, "Sigh. I'm feeling down." The woman in the cream jacket is already leaning toward him with a cup and an instant solution: "Don't stay in! Let's hike!" The next panel moves them straight onto a mountain path, where she points brightly toward the scenery and promises that the fresh air will help while he trails behind with his backpack and answers, "I'm... not there yet." Her care is sincere, but visually it has already become a program he has to keep up with.

The middle panels make that accidental over-helping increasingly funny. A dining table fills with bowls and plates while the woman announces, "A good meal! Food fixes everything!" and the man dryly replies, "I was only sad. Now I have an itinerary too." Then the scene jumps to karaoke: she sings into a microphone with one fist raised while he sits lower in the frame holding another microphone and admits, "I'm honestly tired..." By the lantern-lit street, she is still cheerfully planning tomorrow's exhibition, film, and hot spring. His line, "You're scheduling harder than my job," lands because the supposed break has begun to resemble another demanding workday.

The turning point arrives beside the water at night. Instead of adding one more activity, the woman finally stops and asks, "Wait. What do you actually want?" The answer is almost comically modest compared with everything that came before: "Just walk with me. Sit when we get tired." In panel 07 they simply walk together under the moon, and her reply—"Okay. No more scheduling."—changes the rhythm of the page. Panel 08 briefly shows how strong her old habit still is: she is holding a COMFORT PLAN listing HIKE, DINNER, KARAOKE, and MOVIE and admits, "I nearly added another activity..." He gently answers, "No itinerary today."

Once the schedule disappears, the comic becomes visibly quieter. The pair sit side by side by the moonlit water, each holding a travel mug, and the woman says, "I'll sit with you. No pressure to talk." His "This is much better" is the first clear sign that the kind of company now matches what he asked for. The empty space is not presented as doing nothing, though. In the next panel he chooses a specific kind of help himself: "Later, help me think how to handle tomorrow's phone call." She answers with a much smaller plan—"Walk and sit first. Then an opening sentence." Help has shifted from a universal package to one concrete request.

The final joke turns the whole misunderstanding into a restaurant metaphor. The woman physically puts away a sheet labeled UNIVERSAL COMFORT LIST and says, "No set menu today. You order." The man smiles and replies, "Finally, my taste." In the last panel they remain by the glowing water with their mugs, and he orders exactly what he wants: "One quiet walk. A side of help with tomorrow." She answers, "Coming up. No rushing included." The closing line, "Cancel the set menu. Let company arrive first," connects neatly with Chapter 49 as a limited contemporary reflection: caring for another person can begin by making room for that person's own preference rather than assuming that our favorite remedies automatically fit them.
ask-how-they-want-help.quote: The sage is constantly without a mind of his own; he takes the people's minds as his mind.
ask-how-they-want-help.practice: The next time someone says they are having a hard day, you might delay the ready-made comfort plan and ask, "What would you like me to do with you right now?" If the answer is only a walk, a quiet seat, or help with one specific task later, try following that temporary menu instead.
ask-how-they-want-help.comicAlt: Two-page, twelve-panel English comic in a muted blue-and-gold Nihonga-inspired style. A tousle-haired man in a blue jacket tells a long-haired woman in a cream jacket that he feels down. She enthusiastically takes him hiking, to a large meal, to karaoke, and plans more outings, while he becomes increasingly tired. At a moonlit waterfront she finally asks what he actually wants. He asks only to walk together, sit when tired, and later get help preparing for a phone call. She puts away a written universal comfort list, they sit with mugs beside the water, and the story ends with them joking about replacing the set menu with a quiet walk and one small portion of practical help.

leave-an-avoidable-risk.title: Saving Three Minutes. Risking the Whole Day.
leave-an-avoidable-risk.teaser: Three minutes late, and suddenly a closed path looks like efficiency. A slippery step punctures the shortcut-hero fantasy; an open route, a cat and Bus 318 offer a calmer ending.
paragraphs: The opening joke comes from how quickly the boy turns urgency into permission. He checks his watch, worries that three more minutes will make him late, and the conversation immediately turns to a shortcut. By the next panel, the red-and-white barrier, the large "PATH CLOSED / DETOUR" sign, and the separate "MAINTENANCE / THIS WAY" board make the situation visually unambiguous. The girl points out that the path is closed, but he still answers, "Just a few steps!" The comedy is not that he cannot read the warning; it is that he is already negotiating with it.

That self-justification gets even funnier in panels three and four. When the girl says the detour adds only a few minutes, the boy stands proudly and replies, "I'm not scared. I'm efficient." His imagination then inflates an ordinary commute into a tiny heroic epic: he pictures himself climbing dramatically with a red "FEARLESS" flag while the thought "Real experts never detour" floats above him and "SHORTCUTS ARE COURAGE" appears inside the fantasy. The thought bubble matters because the comic clearly presents this as his private self-image, not as advice from the story.

Reality interrupts the imaginary hero at exactly the right moment. The girl shouts "Wait!" as the boy's shoe skids beside a puddle, with a bright yellow "SLIPPERY" warning sign standing almost comically close by. His "Whoa!" replaces the heroic slogans in an instant. The turning point is deliberately small: in panel six he does not win an argument or perform a dramatic rescue; he simply says, "Let me pull my foot back first." The girl answers, "That's brave enough," while the phone already allows for the practical possibility that they may be a few minutes late.

The lower page makes the detour feel ordinary rather than punitive. The girl points to a sign reading "VIEWPOINT / OPEN PATH / ABOUT 8 MIN," with the closed path clearly marked "NO ENTRY," and says, "This way. A few minutes longer, but open." Soon the boy can joke that the extra walking is a little exercise, and the girl replies, "Arriving safely counts!" They even stop for the visual punch line of a roadside cat: he exclaims "A cat!", the cat contributes a perfectly timed "MEOW," and she reminds him, smiling and holding her phone, "Not too long. We're still on a schedule!"

The ending quietly shrinks the original three-minute crisis back to its proper size. They catch Bus 318, the boy says the trip went smoothly even though they are a little late, and the girl sends a straightforward message: "On our way safely. A few minutes late. Thanks for understanding!" His relieved "Much better" shows that the delay has become something manageable instead of something worth gambling over. In the final panel, warm sunset light fills the bus window as he thinks, "Today's bravest move was stepping back." The closing line, "Some detours come with a better view," links that modest reversal to the supplied Dao De Jing excerpt as a contemporary reflection: not as the one fixed meaning of the ancient text, but as a story about declining an avoidable danger instead of manufacturing one.
leave-an-avoidable-risk.quote: Because there is no place of death there.
leave-an-avoidable-risk.practice: The next time haste, inconvenience, or pride makes a risky shortcut feel strangely reasonable, look first at what the situation is actually telling you: what is closed, what is open, and how much time the safer route really adds. If the difference is only a few minutes, try pulling your foot back before deciding what comes next.
leave-an-avoidable-risk.comicTitle: Saving Three Minutes. Risking the Whole Day.
leave-an-avoidable-risk.comicAlt: A twelve-panel pixel-art comic follows a brown-haired boy in an orange jacket and a girl in a blue hat and blue jacket through a hillside city route. The boy, worried about being late, considers entering a clearly closed path, imagines himself as a fearless shortcut hero, then nearly slips beside a puddle and a slippery warning sign. He steps back, and the pair choose an open route marked as about eight minutes. They walk together, pause briefly for a cat, reach Bus 318, send a message explaining that they will be a few minutes late, and end with the boy sitting on the bus at sunset, thinking that stepping back was his bravest move.
